en: Catalogue of the Zhongnan Family Collection.
Composed by the Iron-Wheel Master (Tiěwēng) of Siming;
compiled by his disciple Xingzhi.
Volume One:
An Essential Compendium of the Teachings on Contemplation; A Drop from the Dust of the Three Contemplations;
Responses to Various Questions on the Teachings and Contemplations by the Japanese Dharma Master Emyō.
Middle Volume:
Text on Receiving the Precepts Again; The True Meaning of the Precept-Substance;
Direct Discourse on the Four Disputes; Essential Treatise; Verses on the Regulation of Robes.
A Treatise on the Divisions of the Saṃgha-body:
An Exegesis of the Section on the Emergence from the Three Realms of Opposites from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*,
with Repeated Openings Based on the Conditions of Feeling.

The Lower Volume: On the Functions of the Mind; On Simultaneously Maintaining Both Observance and Transgression; On the Determination of Offenses through the Establishment of the Retreat; On the Dual Meaning of the Two Restraints; On the Re-explanation of the Eight and Nine Names;
and the Text on "Permeability and Imperviousness" from the Section on Observance and Transgression in the *Shichao* (Commentary on the Essentials).
A Second Response to Master Qin’s Questions on the Analysis of Objects and Perceptions; An Examination of the Four Difficulties Regarding Dreaming and the Maintenance or Violation of Precepts;
A Brief Discernment of the Proper Application of the Two Kinds of Precepts—Causal and Resultant; A Concise Discussion on Mutual Correlation;
Seventh, A Brief Discernment of Non-Substantiality; And a Brief Discussion on the Teaching of Formal Conclusions and Offenses.
*Zhongnan Jiaye*, Scroll One:
*Essentials of Teaching and Contemplation*.

Our Patriarch propagated the Vinaya, taking wondrous contemplation as its foundation. This was based on the Vinaya, wherein the Buddha ordained that bhikṣus should practice mindfulness and contemplation in opposition [to afflictions].

Only through such cultivation can one enter the Way; hence it is said: "Always maintain a single-minded focus, mindful of removing all hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); to deviate from this constitutes a transgression.

However, within the Vinaya, both contemplation and mindfulness are largely provisional and preliminary. The Patriarchs thoroughly investigated the Buddha’s intent and profoundly accorded with the spirit of the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*.

They directly relied upon the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (as cited in the *Gongjing yi*) to realize that objects have no inherent existence (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), thereby attaining penetration into Reality (*paramārtha-satya*). They then realized that consciousness alone exists (*vijñapti-mātratā*).

(Contemplation of the Provisional) penetrates the conventional (the conventional truth). If one does not penetrate the conventional, there is no means to penetrate the ultimate. If one does not penetrate the ultimate, there is no means to dispel the conventional.

Based on the principle that the conventional has no separate essence and so forth (as explained above, the mutual identity of the ultimate and the conventional constitutes the Truth of Emptiness; the non-duality of emptiness and the provisional constitutes the Middle Way), the sublime contemplation of the Middle Way is established as the foundation for the study of those who have left the household life.
This is stated in both the *Sāśī-pǐn* (Chapter on Śrāmaṇeras) of the *Shìshāo* and the *Shòu-jì-pǐn* (Chapter on Receiving Precepts) of the *Yè-sū*.

To contemplate phenomena as being identical to mind: "phenomena" here refers collectively to the ten realms, including the physical environment and its inhabitants, as well as all dharmas such as form and mind.

These are, in fact, originally inherent within the Mind alone; they are entirely the manifestations of the Mind. Phenomena are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the Mind is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

That phenomena and the Mind are neither identical nor separate is the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*). To contemplate phenomena in this manner—how could it be conceived by the intellect? It enabled even a novice śrāmaṇera to open up wondrous understanding.
To realize that phenomena are the principle is for the entirety of nature to become cultivation; whatever is applied in practice all becomes sublime conduct.

Furthermore, in the *Chao-shu* (Commentary on the Vinaya), in the section on the Confession of the Six Groups of Offenses, it says: "External objects among all dharmas fundamentally do not exist; in reality, there is only consciousness. This principle is profound and subtle.

The former phrase refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and the latter phrase refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The conventional does not depart from the ultimate, and the ultimate does not depart from the conventional; they are neither identical nor separate.

"Detachment" is precisely the Middle Truth (wherein it is the object, there are the Three Truths; wherein it is the subject, there are the Three Contemplations). The dharma of the Three Truths is subtle, wondrous, and perfectly interfused;

therefore, it is called "profound and wondrous. When correlating these two preceding passages, their meaning is identical. This means that the one mind is the Three Truths, and the Three Truths are the one mind.
If the one mind is taken as the subject of contemplation, then the Three Truths both belong to the subject of contemplation, constituting the single mind.

The three contemplations are perfectly integrated within the wondrous contemplation. If one takes the single mind as the object of contemplation, then the three truths are likewise all objects of contemplation;

thus, they constitute the wondrous realm where the single mind and the three truths are perfectly integrated. In this state, both the realm and the contemplation are clearly manifest, and the subject and object mutually illuminate one another.

Within the absence of subject and object, subject and object are distinct; within the absence of differentiation, differentiation is vividly present. Furthermore, regarding the ritual of taking refuge and paying homage:
There is nothing that can be honored other than the three types of action (*trikarma*), and there is nothing more worthy of veneration than the Three Jewels (*triratna*).

Within each chapter and every matter, one shall cause principle and phenomena to be perfectly integrated, with the ultimate and conventional truths operating in tandem (the preceding concludes the explanation of contemplation). Since the established contemplation is thus subtle and wondrous, it must necessarily be complete within the teaching.

This school states: "There is no teaching that is not the vehicle of discipline (*vinaya-yāna*). If one were to rely solely on the limitations of the teaching, the discipline would appear partial and deficient; yet when investigating the Buddha’s fundamental intention, all [teachings] are [complete].

All that he has done is for the sake of a single purpose; through hundreds of thousands of skillful means, he has applied subtle effort and mediation—all of which are the Buddha’s provisional strategies.

He spoke according to the inclinations of others until, finally, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, he fully expressed his original intent. By opening and resolving the partial and limited teachings, he revealed the One Buddha Vehicle.

In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he supported the discourse to ultimately manifest the Buddha-nature. From ancient times, the transmission of the Vinaya has been entirely obscure regarding the return to the source; only our Nanshan [Daoxuan] possessed such lofty aspirations.

Zhuo Lang adjudicated the gates of the Śāsanā, ensuring that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*) were not conflated. Relying specifically on two sūtras, he elucidated and supported the wondrous intent [of the Buddha], directly revealing that the precepts and regulations are themselves the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇayāna*).
He pointed out that both objective conditions and the practice of receiving and following the precepts are all identical to the one mind; there is nothing that is not *vijñaptimātra*.
How could this teaching and practice of "Mind-Only" not be perfectly wondrous? Now, I shall further briefly cite various texts so that students may understand.

Regarding its teaching (the following citation from the *Jièfǎchù* [Section on the Precepts] refers specifically to this teaching): as the *Shìchāo* [Commentary on the Essentials] points out regarding the precepts, it says:

"The dharmadhātu and the sands of the Ganges—these are the dharmas of the two truths and so forth. The dharmadhātu is the essence of the precepts; the sands of the Ganges are the numerical aspects of the precepts.

If one takes the dharmadhātu as the object, one must thoroughly understand that object, which is precisely the dharma of the two truths and the three truths. It is not that what is not a 'realm' (dhātu) is called a 'realm'. Thus it is said.
It is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). One should know that the dharma of precepts is established as a provisional designation upon the principle of the Dharma-realm;
therefore, there are distinctions, and their number is equal to the atoms of space or the sands of the Ganges. Thus, it is said to be the dharma of the two truths (*dvayasatya*).

This refers to what is meant when it is said that "the Buddhas, in teaching the Dharma, always rely upon the two truths. The two truths are neither identical nor separate; they are forcibly named the Middle Truth (*madhyamasatya*). Therefore, it is one.

In every teaching gate, the three truths are perfectly interfused; thus, it is a subtle and wondrous Dharma. Therefore, the text continues: "To fathom and contemplate with clear wisdom" (the contemplation of the wondrous) is to correspond with the wondrous Dharma (the wondrousness of the teaching).

"Fathoming and contemplating" refers to the mind that is able to receive; "wondrous Dharma" refers to the Dharma that is received. By means of the subtle and wondrous mind, one receives the subtle and wondrous Dharma.

Since the essence of the subject (the receiver) and the object (the received) are identical, this is the single reality-mark (one *dharmatā*). Hence, it is called "correspondence. — *Chao* (Commentary).
The *Zhong* (the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*) further states: "The characteristics of the precepts that are generated are immeasurable... (and so forth)...

If discussed in terms of their objects, they do not exceed the categories of sentient and non-sentient beings, the two truths of emptiness and existence, the principle of cessation (*nirvāṇa*), the Buddha’s holy teachings, written scrolls, images, stupas, temples, earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, and so on;
taking the entire dharma-realm as their measure, all of these constitute the substance of the precepts. This passage [is from the *Zhong*].
By means of the *dharmadhātu*, one binds together all the aforementioned objects; thus, each and every object is the subtle and wondrous *dharmadhātu*.

Since the various precepts are established in reliance upon the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmadhātu* is the essence (*svabhāva*) of the dharma of the precepts. Therefore, it is said that they are all the substance of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*).

This ensures that the recipient, by means of the mind of the *dharmadhātu*, takes the *dharmadhātu* as the object and receives the dharma of the *dharmadhātu*; there is only this single *dharmadhātu*, without any difference.
The Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is the ultimate single characteristic in which subject and object have vanished. Therefore, it is attained. Furthermore, the *Chao* text states:

"Profound precepts and supreme goodness pervade the Dharma-realm extensively" (*wen*). If the essence of the precept-dharma were not the Dharma-realm itself, how could it be called "profound," and how could it be called "supreme goodness"?

Moreover, the opening of the *Chao* Preface says, "The virtue of the precepts is inconceivable," and so forth. Although this passage praises the merit of the precepts, it does so because their essence is subtle.

Because it is wondrous, its function is inconceivable; scholars are unable to investigate it in this manner, which leads them to suppress the teachings—a circumstance that moves me to profound sorrow.
Furthermore, the *Yejie shu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "When wisdom cognizes objective conditions, they are fundamentally created by the mind; do not falsely take objects as conditions."
However, the single consciousness (text) has objects as its sensory realms (*viṣaya*) and conditions as the precepts (*śīla-dharma*).

Since both the object and the precepts are but the single consciousness, this "consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātra*) is precisely the wondrous principle of the perfect fusion of the three truths (*tri-satya*). How could the object not be wondrous? How could the dharma not be perfect?

Furthermore, it is because those who wish to receive [the precepts] must reach the source and realize the root of consciousness, perfectly giving rise to the supreme mind, perfectly embracing the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-koṭi-śīla*), and perfectly accomplishing the three practices (*tri-caryā*). Therefore...
The Commentary further states: "Constantly contemplating this practice is itself the restraint of the precepts (śīla-saṃvara), which serves as the Dharma-Buddha and is the pure mind.
This practice is the 'lesser dharma,' while the restraint is the Mahāyāna; the Dharma-Buddha is the fruition-virtue. Thus, the lesser is the greater, and the cause is the fruition.
The lesser, the greater, the cause, and the fruition are all one pure mind, without distinction. Therefore, the Commentary further says: "The Lesser and the Greater..."
The shared mind and the non-differentiation of the precepts are extremely clear in their meaning; the perfect phrasing and subtle significance are fully contained within the various texts.
Yet, those who study without investigating the heart rarely succeed in grasping the essentials. My ancestral teachings and contemplations have nearly been swept from the ground.

I once explained the five gates of the Perfect Teaching and answered the doubts of the Japanese Master Enchō in works such as *The Three Contemplations* and *Dust and Dew*, where I ventured to express my own limited views.
I have set aside the sacred words for fear that their prolixity might make them difficult for students to comprehend.

I have now extracted the essential meaning and recorded it separately on this single sheet, hoping it will facilitate its circulation and serve as a path for extensive investigation. This is by no means an attempt to purchase reputation or seek fame;

rather, it is my sincere wish that my fellow students will study with precision and investigate exhaustively, so that they may, first, benefit themselves and, second, transform others, ensuring both accord with reality and do not bring shame upon our tradition.
Yi. On the day before the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa in the *Ren-yin* year of the Chunyou era, [this text] was brought forth from beneath the Huayan Pavilion.

The Three Contemplations are like a drop of dew to our Ancestor, Great Master Nanshan Chengzhao. His traces manifest as the Four Reliances; his rank is that of the Highest Ground (*uttama-bhūmi*). He is the wondrously luminous single reality.

He thoroughly penetrated both vehicles; his literary style was held in high esteem as he participated in the translation assemblies, and celestial dragons attended him in reverence as he presided over the lecture halls.

Lamenting that the Vinaya-piṭaka is truly the lifeblood of the Buddha-dharma, and moved by the fact that the virtue of the precepts is the very foundation of concentration and wisdom, he devoted himself single-mindedly to its propagation throughout three lifetimes.

He challenged the six heretical teachers and widely disseminated the texts. Although the entire school regards the principles of observance and violation as paramount, [he ensured their correct transmission].
In this work, both principle and contemplation are clarified through cultivation; merit and wisdom are practiced in tandem; and both transformation and regulation are shown to be equally received.

Relying comprehensively upon the two canons, the three stages are listed in their entirety. While its meaning encompasses all aspects, its phrasing is concise; how could my narrow vision ever exhaust it?

How can superficial reception ever reach its limit? Only the Master of the *Lingzhi ji*, the Great Wisdom Vinaya Master, has profoundly investigated the true source and deeply researched the flavor of principle.
His discipline followed the tradition of Nanfu, yet his teaching was led by Nanping; his station was secluded at West Lake, yet his Way resounded throughout India.

He extensively elucidated the practice of the Perfect [Teaching] and wondrously expounded the texts of Contemplation; he analyzed the shallow and the deep, his brilliance illuminating both past and present. (Shouyi) humbly follows in his footsteps of study.

I, your humble servant, have merely sought out the textual characteristics; my ignorant mind harbors many reservations. I have briefly elucidated the meaning and resolved discrepancies in other traditions, hoping this may slightly aid my own understanding.

I am ashamed that my capacity is as narrow as a small measure and my insight as lowly as a firefly’s glow. Though I have exhausted my sincerity, how could I possibly exhaust the underlying principles?
They are like dust and dew compared to the mountains and seas; therefore, I have titled this work *The Dust and Dew of the Three Contemplations*. It is divided into four major sections.
First, citing the original text; second, providing a brief explanation; third, indicating the underlying intent; fourth, resolving differences with other traditions.

First, citing the original text: The *Sìchāo* (Chapter on Repentance) states: "First, the nature of all phenomena is empty and without self; when this principle illuminates the mind, it is called the Hīnayāna.
Second, the fundamental characteristics of all phenomena are empty; they are merely false perceptions of the deluded mind; when this principle illuminates..."

[The first] application belongs to the small *bodhisattvas*. Thirdly, all external objects of the various dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; in reality, there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
This principle is profound and subtle, known only through mental apprehension (*manas-pratyaya*); it is the realized practice of the fruit of Buddhahood for great *bodhisattvas*.

Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states: "Consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) pervades the four stages," and so forth. Furthermore, the *Shishi yaolan* (in the *Śrāmaṇera* section) and the *Jieshu* (in the *Upasaṃpadā* section) likewise state: First, the followers of the Small Vehicle [perceive that] when they perform contemplation, phenomena arise.
1. Extinction (*nirodha*): knowing that there is no self, person, or the nature of good and evil, etc. 2. The practice of the small *bodhisattva*: contemplating the arising and ceasing of phenomena;

knowing that there is no self, person, or the characteristics of good and evil, etc. (The *Yebao yezhang chanyuan yigui shu* says: "contemplating that phenomena are empty," etc.). 3. The practice of the great *bodhisattva*: contemplating that phenomena are mind;

because they are conceptualizations of mental discourse (*manojalpa*). Thus, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "From the stage of zealous application (*adhimukti-caryā*) up to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-gata*), it is called 'contemplation' (*vipaśyanā*)."

It takes the conceptualization of mental discourse as its object. Furthermore, the *Karmasūtra* (Chapter on Repentance) states: "At the ultimate limit of the Hīnayāna, there are the two contemplations of person and phenomena.

When one contemplates by analyzing in relation to the self, one sees only external objects (*viṣaya*). When one seeks within the aggregates (*skandha*), there are merely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). When seeking the person or seeking phenomena..."

It is utterly unobtainable; this is what is meant by emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This is the ultimate point of the Mahāyāna: emptiness and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are its foundation. Beginners, being hindered by shallow teachings, claim that external objects are empty;

yet when one realizes that objects are fundamentally non-existent, their nature is seen to be consciousness alone. (The *Jìngxīn jièguān guījìng yí* [Protocol for Reverence and Contemplation of the Pure Mind] provides a detailed explanation of contemplation according to principle; therefore, it is not recorded here in full.)

The second part, the section on exposition, has two divisions. First, the summary of the general intent: Examining the various texts mentioned above, none fail to indicate the essence of contemplation through the ultimate principle of the three stages (*tri-krama*).
However, regarding the mental objects, the modes of activity, and the specific characteristics of practice, these are all treated briefly in those texts.

A comprehensive account is found in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) and the *Method for the Practice of Ordinary and Holy Beings* by Master Daozheng, both of which were widely circulated at that time; therefore, the aforementioned texts all refer back to them.
The writings of Master Zhizhe have largely been lost in recent times. The meaning of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) is difficult for beginners to comprehend.

The various records of Lingzhi further indicate that the *Tiantai Mohe zhiguan* is where one may entrust one’s mind. This is because the commentaries and sub-commentaries of this school primarily clarify the rules of observance and transgression (*dhāraṇa* and *atikrama*), as well as the cultivation of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi* and *prajñā*).
It was necessary to provide supplementary indications, yet fearing they might confuse the path of the school, they were not expanded upon extensively. Next, the commentary is explained.

The textual structure. Dividing the text according to its phrasing, there are three sections: namely, the object (*viṣaya*), the principle (*tattva*), and the person (*pudgala*). First, the indication of the object.

All three contemplations refer to "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) and speak of "contemplating things. If we consider them in relation to the capacities of the practitioners (*yogācāra*), their scope must be distinguished as broad or narrow. Regarding the first, the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), the capacity of the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is narrow;

for them, "all phenomena" refers only to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the six classes of ordinary beings. As for the latter two contemplations, they specifically point to the ten contemplations, which encompass all three [vehicles].

In this world, all phenomena (*dharma*) are thus. Furthermore, whenever the mind moves toward an object, whatever is thought of is a phenomenon. These phenomena and objects encompass both the internal and the external.

When one grasps at objects and forms karma, there is nothing that exceeds false conceptualization (*parikalpa*). The first two [of the three types of objects] refer to "self" and "person," while the last one refers to "mental verbalization";

all are instances of false conceptualization. By setting aside the remote and focusing on the proximate, it is precisely false conceptualization that is designated as the object of observation. Therefore...

The *Record* states: "Third, by illuminating the principle, one comes to know that inversion consists merely of false conceptualization. It further states: "One simply refutes false conceptualization. And it says:

"This refers to the contemplation of the nature [of phenomena], and so forth" (the preceding section on the object has concluded). Regarding the second point, "principle": principle is the essence of contemplation, and it is also the essence of all phenomena.

If we follow the literal indications of the text, these are emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*), emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), selflessness (*anātman*), and consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*) as mind, and so forth.

This is so. Although the textual passages are divided and there are distinctions between the objective realm (*viṣaya*) and its underlying principle (*tattva*), in reality the phrases and meanings are continuous;

all phenomena (*dharmas*) are identical with the principle and cannot be differentiated. One must know that all phenomena are but the single mind, ultimately perfect and luminous, a single mark of equality.

Through false conceptualization, one obstructs oneself and becomes greedily attached to saṃsāra. Accordingly, the Tathāgata, following the capacities of sentient beings, sometimes teaches that all phenomena are empty.
Some say that there is only the single true reality (*dharmatā*). Because the faculties of those in the Hīnayāna are inferior, they take emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to be the ultimate;

among them, those of duller capacity must analyze the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) before they perceive the principle of emptiness, whereas those of sharper capacity realize that phenomena are themselves empty. Later, within the Mahāyāna, there is likewise one class [of practitioners].

Although they have aroused the great mind (*mahācitta*), they have not yet fathomed the root of the mind; they merely recognize emptiness as the ultimate principle. Their understanding that appearances are themselves empty differs from the former [stage].

Because their vows and aspirations are vast and great, they are called Bodhisattvas. Among those who cultivate *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), there are none who lack either sharp or dull faculties.

Those of dull faculties practice separately; they enter from the conventional into emptiness before finally reaching the Middle Way. Those of sharp faculties enter perfectly, such that the beginning and the end are as one, and both cause and effect are wondrous.
To clarify this further, a question is raised: Regarding the two kinds of emptiness—of nature and of characteristics—do they only empty the self and persons, or do they also empty all phenomena?
The *Chao* (Excerpts) text mentions only "no-self" (*anātman*) and does not speak of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Please explain this for us. Answer: The text contains it in full.

[The interlocutor] says: "How is it not detailed? First, it is said that 'the nature of all phenomena is empty'; this refers to the emptiness of the essence-nature of phenomena. Next, it is said that 'non-self is emptiness';

this refers to the emptiness of the nature of grasping at a self and a person. Following that, it is said that 'the characteristics of all phenomena are empty'; this refers to the emptiness of the characteristic-essence of phenomena."
It further states: "Non-self" means the emptiness of the marks of attachment to self and person. It also says: "Contemplating the arising and ceasing of phenomena" refers to the emptiness of dharmas.

To know there is no self or person is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Thus, there are two types of emptiness—of nature and of characteristics—which together encompass both persons and dharmas.

This is very clear in the *Yebao jing yishu* (Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra) and even more evident in the *Jiwen* (Recorded Text). Furthermore, the meaning of persons and dharmas is extensively set forth in various texts; students should understand this for themselves. Herein...

(No need for further elaboration, as it has already been briefly explained in the *Jueyi zhuan*). One must understand that in terms of the objective realm (*viṣaya*), these are the two attachments to persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*); in terms of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), they are the two wisdoms regarding persons and phenomena;

and in terms of principle (*tattva*), they are the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena. Question: Both the *Xingguan* (Contemplation of Nature) and the *Xiangguan* (Contemplation of Characteristics) are described in the *Chao* (Commentary) as being "arising and ceasing" (*utpāda-nirodha*).
How are they distinguished? Answer: In the former, one perceives characteristics as they truly are, arising and ceasing in dependence upon conditions. In the latter, one perceives...
Phenomena are like illusions, like flowers in the sky or the moon reflected in water; they arise and perish in emptiness. Initially, arising and perishing are taken as real;

subsequently, arising and perishing are seen as empty. Thus, the *Yejue* (Commentary on Rituals) says: "To contemplate that phenomena are empty" is precisely this point. The text states: "External objects are fundamentally non-existent."
"Reality is only consciousness. These two phrases constitute the perfect fusion of the three truths, the wondrous principle of the Middle Way.

"Dust" refers to all phenomena, as they are all comprised within the six sense-objects. In contrast to ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, who do not understand the source of the mind, these are called "external.

"Fundamental" (ben) means the original source; "without" (wu) refers to the essence of reality; "real" (shi) means not false; and "only" (wei) is glossed as "exclusive. The two characters "fundamental" and "real" manifest [this meaning].
To understand its essential meaning, I shall now provide three interpretations to explain these two lines. First, the interpretation by defining the essence:

All dharmas, from the very beginning, whether in their substance or their characteristics, have had their traces obliterated and their forms vanished; they are ultimately like space, subtle and beyond measure.

This is precisely the one True Suchness, wherein there is nothing that is not the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi). Therefore, it is said that external objects are fundamentally non-existent; this is because they are entirely inherent within the Mind-only.
The mind arises; all phenomena are mind, and every sensory object is consciousness. This is the ultimate instruction, hence it is said that in reality there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*).
Consciousness is the perfect principle, yet its essence is fundamentally non-existent. Thus, non-existence is consciousness, and consciousness is non-existence.

Furthermore, regarding the substance of all phenomena, we speak figuratively of "non-existence"; regarding the characteristics of all phenomena, we provisionally establish the term "consciousness. Non-existence is thus consciousness.

The essence is the substance of this, while consciousness is its characteristic. They are neither identical nor separate, and furthermore, they are inconceivable; thus, they are said to be wondrous and profound. Second, the interpretation that dispels emotional attachments:

to speak of "originally non-existent" is to dispel the attachment to existence and its conceptual reckonings. Although original non-existence is empty, this emptiness is not a partial or biased emptiness.
The provisional designation of consciousness is itself the sublime existence (*pranīta-bhāva*). It does not cling to the two extremes, nor is it separate from the two extremes;

this is the Middle Way. Therefore, it is called "sublime. Third, the explanation by way of cultivation: according to the *Liang* translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, within the stage of expedient means (*upāya*), one first uses the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) to eliminate the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
One perceives that all objects (*viṣaya*) are empty and devoid of essence, consisting merely of mental-linguistic conceptualization (*manojalpa-vikalpa*). Thus...
It is said that external objects are fundamentally non-existent; thus, the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is inverted into the nature of signlessness (*animitta-lakṣaṇa*).

Here, "non-existence" refers merely to perceiving the emptiness of objects (which constitutes the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness). Although the essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is indeed consciousness-only, because wisdom has not yet been sharpened, one perceives only its semblance.

By means of the nature of reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the dependent nature is eliminated; as the nature of reality gradually manifests, the dependent nature gradually dissolves. Thereafter, [the single...]
All phenomena resemble names, resemble objects, and resemble mere consciousness; they neither arise nor cease from anywhere.

Through the conceptualization of mental discourse, one attains non-conceptual wisdom, which overturns the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) into the nature of non-arising. Herein, the term "non-existence" precisely indicates the essence of consciousness.

(The provisional contemplation is thus perfected. The essence of true reality is the *dharmatā* (real mark). Originally there is nothing to be overturned; yet, wishing to manifest the subtlety of this essence, one overturns "the nature of having no nature" (*niḥsvabhāva-svabhāva*) and speaks of "the nature of that which has no nature.

This reveals that emptiness is precisely consciousness (thus the middle contemplation is perfected). Only here is the perfect and subtle awakening of *Vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) fully manifested;

only here is the ultimate perfection seen. The sequence of the preceding treatises was not intended to establish this present position. True and conventional [truths] operate simultaneously; emptiness and the provisional [are unified].

This is precisely the middle way. The three natures are cultivated in perfect unity; both the beginning and the end are wondrous. This is the core tenet of our school, as will be further clarified below. Question: The text contains only two phrases.
How can one see therein the meaning of the perfect fusion of the three truths (*trisatya*) and the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*)? Answer:

That external objects are fundamentally non-existent is the Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārthasatya*), which is also the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). That, in reality, only consciousness exists is the Truth of Conventional Reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*), which is also the contemplation of the provisional (*upādāya-prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
Contemplation: consciousness itself is non-existent; emptiness does not depart from the conventional. That which is neither identical to nor separate from [the conventional] is called the Middle Way.

Thus one should know that the establishment of contemplation relies solely upon the perfect fusion of the three truths and the wondrous principle of the Middle Way. Therefore, the text concludes: "This principle is profound and subtle—is this not so?

This is precisely in accordance with the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (as cited in the section on "Respectful Conduct"), which states: "Knowing that objects have no existence is to penetrate the Truth" (the "Truth" being the Truth of Ultimate Reality).

Knowing non-existence is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Knowing that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) is the penetration of the conventional; "the conventional" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and knowing consciousness is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*).

If one does not penetrate the conventional, there is no means to penetrate the ultimate (*paramārtha*). (The former means that when penetrating the ultimate, one must first penetrate the conventional as empty. If one does not penetrate the ultimate, there is no means to dispel the conventional, because the conventional has no separate essence.

(The former means that when penetrating the conventional, one must first penetrate the ultimate as being the conventional itself. The first two lines separately indicate the objects of contemplation; the latter two lines [indicate] the actual...
This reveals the perfect cultivation. Our Patriarch established the Perfect Contemplation based on this treatise. The *Commentary* further states:

"The contemplation that phenomena are mind" refers to the three truths as a whole; it demonstrates the wondrous principle. Since all objective phenomena are merely mind and arise through conditions, they are empty. All things are provisional;
since they are both empty and identical to mind, they do not depart from the provisional. Is this not so?

Is this not the Middle Way? If one understands this meaning, then both the object and the contemplation are as such; cause and faculty are both wondrous. As an object, it is the wondrous object of the Middle Way;
as a principle, it is the wondrous principle of the Middle Way; as contemplation, it is the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way.

This is the Patriarch’s summary of the perfect meaning within the *Jin'gang xian lun* (The Diamond Scalpel Treatise), establishing the perfect contemplation to be applied in perfect cultivation, from the initial arousal of the mind until the end.
Reaching the ultimate, one wondrously masters mental discourse (*manojalpa*); there is nothing that is not the Middle Way. Therefore, it is said:

"From the stage of aspiration and delight (*adhimukti*) to the ultimate stage, this is called 'contemplating the object of the Middle. Mental discourse and conceptualization serve as the objective realm. (Regarding the interpretation of this "Middle" according to other schools as merely referring to the "Middle [Truth]" alone: this is likely because they have not thoroughly investigated the treatise nor grasped the intent of the Patriarchs.

Within the treatise, there is further the meaning of "Perfection" (*pariniṣpanna*); I shall now briefly cite and clarify it. The treatise uses gold hidden within earth as a metaphor for the three [natures].

Regarding the three natures (the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected), Tiantai says that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* passage concerning "dyeing gold with clay" expresses the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].

This refers to the meaning of the perfect cultivation of the three natures within the stage of skillful means characterized by aspiration and delight as discussed in the *Śāstra*. The *Śāstra* further states: "There are two kinds of bodhisattvas:

first, those in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); second, those in the stage of sages (*ārya*). From the initial generation of the mind of awakening until the completion of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), all belong to the stage of ordinary beings.
From the ten understandings (*daśa-adhimukti*) upward, all are included within the stage of sages" (the ten understandings are equivalent to the ten abidings). This is also from the *Śāstra*.

This is from the "Middle" [section]. It is the passage concerning the initial dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) where delusions are shattered and the holy state is realized. The treatise further states: "Regarding all phenomena, in reality there is only consciousness;

within the principle (the mental verbalization), conceptual discrimination arises, and so forth. This, too, is the perfected meaning within the treatise. "Within the principle" refers to the skillful means of the essence itself.
"Principle" is the wondrous principle; "middle" is the Middle Way; and "mental verbalization and conceptual discrimination" refers to the contemplation of the initial stage.

By perceiving the object, one immediately penetrates the subtle principle of the Middle Way; is this not the meaning of perfect cultivation? In the *Guijing yi* (Ritual of Homage), after establishing "perfect contemplation," an opponent raises an objection:
"I have heard that the simultaneous contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional is practiced only upon reaching the [first] stage (*bhūmi*).

How can an ordinary person of the lower realms presume to equal the sages of the higher stages? (This refers to those in the ten stages as "sages" and those prior to the ten faiths as "ordinary persons"). The first master answers himself: "The aspiration is perfected..."
[The preceding section] concludes. From the initial to the final mind, they are equal; one must not cling to the literal text, for to do so would deviate from the reality of the meaning and so forth.

According to this text, prior to the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), from the very first arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*), one cultivates the perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-vipaśyanā*) without any difference from what follows.

This is identical to what was previously cited from the treatise: "From the stage of aspiration (*adhimukti-avasthā*) to the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*)," etc.; there is no distinction in their meaning. Such is the brief indication.

Thus, the commentaries and sub-commentaries establish the meditative contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) based on the "perfect" (*pariniṣpanna*) meaning within the treatise, as they are intended for perfect cultivation.

The masters of recent times have not been adept at their investigation; they falsely claim that the "external objects," "consciousnesses," and "mental verbalizations" mentioned in the text refer only to the characteristics of the contemplations practiced during the stage of "aspiration and delight" (*adhimukti*), and should not be understood as applying to subsequent stages. This is because that treatise, within this particular stage, teaches...

The correct contemplation of "images as mere consciousness" (vijñaptimātra) involves using mental verbalization (*manojalpa*) to eliminate and suppress external objects; it is only upon reaching the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) that one attains the Middle Way.
This interpretation by various masters—relying on the literal text to explain the meaning—is a severe suppression of the Master’s [Asaṅga’s] intent.

For they do not realize that the treatise contains both the complete (*pariniṣpanna*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*) meanings, which respectively apply to those of sharp and dull faculties, and are intended for those possessing both the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) and the delight (*ruci*). Thus, passages concerning mental verbalization, the elimination of objects, and so forth, pertain to the practice of those with dull faculties.

This refers to the distinct meanings [of the teachings]. The positions established in the *Shu* and *Chao* rely exclusively on the *Yuan* (Perfect) texts, as briefly cited previously; the meaning is indeed clear.

Yet, within the *Guijing Yi* (Ritual of Taking Refuge and Paying Homage), the distinctions between the Perfect and Distinct, and between the sharp and dull faculties, as well as the slowness or speed of cultivation and progress, are all fully elucidated in accordance with the treatise.
As cited below in the *Ming*: "The text states: 'This principle illuminates the mind. Regarding 'the function of illumination,' the principle is itself the contemplation (*guan*).
The principle is that which illuminates, while the mind and its function are both that which is illuminated. Question: The *Zizhi* states:

"If, during the course of practice, the contemplation of the mind is essential, then whether [an action] is good or evil, the three principles illuminate it. Thus, all three are illuminating the mind; why then is only the initial contemplation [so designated]?"

Yes. The answer is: It is precisely because spiritual capacities vary between sharp and dull that their modes of contemplation differ. Although both illuminate the mind, there is a distinction between the comprehensive and the limited.

Those of the Two Vehicles possess dull capacities; they contemplate only the deluded mind to eliminate attachment to a self and persons. Even if there are phenomenal functions, they merely illuminate this [deluded] mind.

This causes delusions not to arise; thus, upon reaching the stage of fruition, even when benefiting others, one does so solely by illuminating the mind while abiding in the principle of empty quiescence.

Therefore, the *Zizhi* states: "The two vehicles abide in quiescence and therefore only illuminate the mind; the practice of the lesser bodhisattvas involves benefiting others in succession according to their capacities."
Although it also illuminates the mind, it does not merely consist of exclusive adherence; for its aspiration to benefit others is vast, and its functional applications are manifold.

It constantly illuminates these functional applications, wherein their very characteristics are identical to emptiness. Thus, the *Zizhi* states: "Because Bodhisattvas engage with phenomena, it is called 'illuminating function.

Some say that because it previously emptied the deluded attachments to self and person, it was called 'illuminating the mind'; now, because it empties the provisional application of the five aggregates as a harmonious combination, [it is called 'illuminating function']."

Regarding the statement that "it illuminates function": such an interpretation is likely incorrect. One must understand that while characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are empty, one must also empty the deluded attachments of the self and persons (*pudgala*).

Have you not seen it stated in the *Chao* (Commentary): "Knowing that there are no characteristics of self, person, good, evil, and so forth"? And again: "The fundamental characteristics are empty; it is only through deluded attachment that they are perceived as such"?

Those who have attained realization should examine this further in detail. Question: Why does the subsequent "Observation of Consciousness-Only" (*Vijñaptimātra-vipaśyanā*) not mention "illumination"?

Answer: The former two faculties are dull; one must apply the mind to reflect upon them before they can become empty. The latter, however, possesses sharp wisdom and deeply understands the subtle principle;

since its negation and illumination are beyond duality and subject and object are perfectly integrated, what need is there for illumination? If this is so, why does the *Zizhi* (The Supporter) speak of "illuminating" it? Answer:

This is merely a general indication for the time being, as all three are said to involve "illumination. Upon reaching the later section on Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*), although the sense of "illumination" still exists, [it is understood differently].

Since the understanding of wisdom is subtle, it illuminates without being an illumination; therefore, while illuminating, it is eternally quiescent, and while quiescent, it is eternally illuminating. Thus, the name "illumination" is not established. The *Yejie shu* (Commentary on the Ritual) states:
"When observing and analyzing in relation to the self, one sees only these objects (*dharmas*). The *Ji* (Sub-commentary) explains: "The 'self' here refers to the *dharma-āyatana*.

One must know that there are two kinds of *dharma-āyatana*: first, the residual impressions of the five sensory objects; second, the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) such as the notions of self and person."

False conceptualization (*parikalpa*) is essentially a mental activity; as it is a derivative of the mind (*caitta*), it belongs to the object-field of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). Alternatively, "object-field" (*viṣaya*) may be understood as "objective sphere.
This is because when one observes and evaluates in relation to an objective sphere, that sphere falls within the category of the phenomenon-object-field (*dharmaviṣaya*).

Some say: the notions of "self" (*ātman*) and "person" (*pudgala*) are merely arbitrary attachments arising upon the substantial basis of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). When one now seeks for this self or person, they have no inherent essence; one perceives only the aggregate of form.

It is merely that the dust-particles (*rajas*) are large. Next, one seeks the dust-particles of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the other four aggregates through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā*).

One sees only name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), as stated in that text; regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), one should examine it more closely. Question: How are "contemplation" (*guan*) and "principle" (*li*) distinguished? Answer: To speak in terms of their essential nature (*tattva*):

Contemplation (*guan*) is itself the principle (*li*). Alternatively, one may distinguish between cause and effect, or the difference between subject and object; there is indeed a specific intent to this. When it pertains to the cause, it is called "viewing" (*shi*);
when it pertains to the fruit, it is called "principle. Furthermore, contemplation is the act of contemplating, while principle is that which is revealed.

Question: How, moreover, are contemplation and practice (*xing*) distinguished? Answer: Contemplation is the ultimate principle, its essence transcending words and thought. Practice is the active mind, involving cultivation and actualization.
If one contemplates without practice, there is no means by which it can be manifested; if one practices without contemplation, there is no means by which it can be perfected.

When understanding and practice are brought together, they support one another like the eye and the foot. (The preceding exposition of principle is concluded. Third, as for "pointing to persons," this refers to the Three Vehicles. The first contemplation is termed the "Lesser Vehicle" (*hīnayāna*), which comprehensively includes both *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
The latter two are termed "Bodhisattvas," further distinguished into the Great and Small [Vehicles]. Question: Regarding the Bodhisattva of the Lesser Vehicle...

In the passage beginning with "Sa" (薩), there are those who appear to be practitioners of meditation (*vipaśyanā*) and those who cite individuals who have attained the fruit (*phala-pudgala*) to clarify the principle (*tattva*).

How, then, can these be definitively determined? Answer: If one relies on the *Shuchao* (疏鈔) in the section on Repentance (*chān*), the establishment of the contemplation based on its essential nature (*ti*) refers exclusively to the ultimate principle (*paramārtha-tattva*). As it says:

"The great essentials of this principle are such that, because these three principles are equal, the three types of individuals who have attained the fruit are cited to manifest the depth or shallowness of the three principles. This refers to the subsequent stage.
Regarding the repeated indication of the Bodhisattva’s Buddha-fruit: first, it reveals that [the path] is not partial; second, it manifests its perfect consummation.

As for the *Śrāmaṇera-varga* (as seen in the commentary on receiving the precepts), it demonstrates contemplation based on practice; thus, the "Small Vehicle Bodhisattvas" are precisely those who cultivate contemplation.
Is it not as it says: "First, the person of the Small Vehicle... and so forth? The *Ji* (Commentary) explains the *Pratideśanā-varga*, stating: "Holding up the profound stage... with the intent to...

The manifestation of the subtle principle does not obstruct the established path. Question: As shown in the text, if contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is based on the ultimate principle and is further termed "sacred activity" (*āryakarma*), which can be cultivated by those in deep stages, does this mean that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have no share in it?
Answer: Although contemplation is the principle itself, its practice (*caryā*) extends to both ordinary beings and sages.

For example, followers of the Hīnayāna must first hear the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) before employing the contemplation of emptiness to traverse various phenomenal aspects (*lakṣaṇa*). When the practice is subtle and the contemplation is dim, [one merely] perceives...

Because the principle has not yet been clarified, one’s status remains that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and practice belongs merely to the realm of phenomena. When contemplation becomes clear and the principle is revealed, one realizes the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).

Only when contemplation accords with the principle is practice termed "noble activity" (*āryakarma*). Subsequently, the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is cultivated throughout all four stages. If one possesses the capacity for perfect realization and attains the highest level, [the stages are traversed accordingly].
By means of contemplation, one perceives the principle that the beginning and the end are identical. As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are termed "sacred" (*ārya*);

from this point onward, all are termed "sacred activities" (*āryakarma*). Whether a person of dull faculties or sharp cultivation practices according to their prior aspirations, even if they contemplate emptiness and existence, they have not yet seen the Middle Way and thus remain in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Only upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) does one first attain the title of "sacred"; the practice is then called sacred activity. This text cites the underlying principle.

Contemplation is called the "noble activity" (ārya-karma). What prevents one from practicing and honoring it? [This concludes the instruction for others. Furthermore, it is said that the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She lun) demonstrates what emerges from the subsequent contemplation.
There are many translations of the original commentary; I have produced a diagram to illustrate them.

Question: As there have been many translations as mentioned above, upon which text do you now rely? Answer: The translation by Paramārtha of the Liang dynasty is that which we now follow as our authority.

Question: Where does the text clearly state that it follows the Liang version? Answer: It is established by our patriarchs that the *Yuanguan zhengben* (Original Text of Perfect Contemplation) contains the passage:

"The Liang version states that objects are non-existent, and one penetrates the equality of reality," and so forth. Furthermore, the *Chao* (Excerpts) says: "From the stage of aspiration and joy up to the ultimate stage..."
The "stages" (*bhūmi*) and so forth are also extracted from that treatise. If this is the Tang recension, the first stage is named "Practice through Resolute Understanding" (*adhimukti-caryā*);

it is said that one exclusively generates resolute understanding (*adhimukti*) in accordance with what has been heard. Therefore, in the Liang recension, the first stage is named "Aspiration and Joy" (*pranidhāna-ruci*), also called "Faith and Joy.

The treatise states: "Relying on this object, one enters the stage of faith and joy through the aspiration and joy of the mind. Since the text says "aspiration and joy," the Liang tradition is clearly established as the primary school. If...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) and its five stages of cultivation and realization differ from this [text]. Question: During the Liang and Tang dynasties, both the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* were circulated concurrently.

With what intention did the Patriarch [Zhiyi] exclusively rely upon the Liang version of the *She lun*? Answer: The various patriarchs each have their own intended focus in their lineages of succession.

For example, when Tiantai presented his contemplative practices (*guan*), he relied upon the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. Nevertheless, the Tang version of the *She lun* and other treatises were translated by the same person as Nanshan [Daoxuan].

The translations produced by [Paramārtha] were concise; those who utilized them were few. The translations by Paramārtha, however, possess perfect principle and sublime practice, deeply accords with the Master’s (Zu) intention;

therefore, they have been widely adopted and utilized. Question: The establishment of the three contemplations applies generally to both vehicles. Why is it that the final contemplation is exclusively associated with the *She dasheng lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty?
Answer: Regarding the characteristics of the contemplative practice (*yogācāra*) based on principle, the sūtras merely provide a general explanation.

Therefore, the various masters of the treatises extensively followed the many scriptures to establish their own schools, demonstrating the essence and instituting the practices so that the various branches and currents would have a point of convergence. Thus, what we now take as our primary authority is, in its broad sense, the Mahāyāna of the entire dispensation;

in its specific sense, it is the first two contemplative practices of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* from the Liang dynasty. As for the teachings upon which this is based, they will be briefly discussed later in the section resolving differences between traditions.
This shall be clarified.
Third, regarding the demonstration of the intended meaning, there are two parts: namely, the general and the specific. First, as for the general meaning:

our ancestors who expounded the *vinaya* and contemplated the ultimate principle did so with profound intent. This was because the teachings established by the Buddha extend downward even to the three... [text continues]
They return to the ten wholesome paths; there are none who are not encompassed by the three vehicles. Their cultivation and study are for the benefit of achieving liberation.

This is especially true regarding the rules for bhikṣus concerning clothing, food, the four modes of deportment, speech, silence, movement, and stillness—they must always maintain a single-minded focus, mindful of removing the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

To violate these is to commit an offense. Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "The precepts were established for the sake of the Path; they are fundamentally not for worldly merit. The precepts are the practice of phenomena (*dharma*), not something dependent upon principle (*li*)."
Wisdom. What is meant by "cultivating the Way"? Furthermore, the expression "cultivating the Way" encompasses meanings at both deep and shallow levels.

If one follows the limitations of the Vinaya teachings, it is said that the increased training in morality (*śīla*) was established for the sake of seeking the four fruits of the śramaṇa. If one investigates the Buddha’s intent, it is for the purpose of accomplishing the single reality (*ekayāna*).

The patriarchs who propagated and elucidated [the Dharma] also took this sacred mind as their foundation. Were it not so, how could one escape the censure of "counting jewels," and how could one hope to be exempted from it?

Is this not a charge of mere exhaustion? I shall simply take the teachings as the occasion for inquiry. These teachings possess both sharp and dull capacities, and their principles range from partial to perfect.

I shall briefly distinguish three stages to clarify the differences between the teachings, and precisely examine the intent of the Patriarchs. This lies solely in not being limited by [the dualistic categories of] nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-dharma-lakṣaṇa*), but in perfectly cultivating *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only).
In this way, may the five groups of monastics receive and uphold these various practices, so that every aspect of their daily conduct and ritual observances shall—

This accords with the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The texts of our own school demonstrate that clear observation reveals the underlying principle, thereby guiding one toward acceptance and compliance;

this meaning is evident throughout various writings, and thus I shall briefly cite them. Accordingly, the *Shishi yaolue chao* states: "To fathom and contemplate with penetrating wisdom is to darkly harmonize with the prior Dharma, to correspond with that wondrous Dharma, and to cause the arousal of the [bodhi-]mind.
This refers exclusively to the superior grade (*adhimātra*). Now, what is this superior-grade mind if not the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*)?

Furthermore, the *Yejieshu* (Exposition of Karma) states: "Wisdom knows that the conditions of objects are originally created by the mind; do not falsely take objects as conditions, but [realize] there is only consciousness alone.

These passages all demonstrate how the practitioner should use wondrous contemplation to harmonize and integrate the aforementioned phenomena, so that subject and object become one in essence, reaching ultimate subtlety.

Furthermore, the *Xian suixing* (Manifesting the Practice According to Conduct) says: "One who aspires to this practice (referring to the minor practices of the *pātimokkha*) is, in fact, practicing the Threefold Aggregate (the Great Vehicle)."

This refers to "riding upon the perfect practice. It further states: "Now, one recognizes that previous conditions (referring here to having already received the *pien-chu* [aggregate] precepts) ultimately lead back to the Mahāyāna;

therefore, one must focus the mind upon the locus (taking the single, true, and wondrous principle as the point of ultimate return). Furthermore, summarizing the source of the teachings, it says: "The intent is solely to rescue and uplift a single person, with the aim of manifesting a single principle.
This is the application of the wisdom of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): receiving the minor precepts is itself the great precept, by means of the true mark."
Hui-chi: Vinaya practice is itself sublime conduct (*sucarita*). Once wisdom and understanding are clear, there is no dharma that is not sublime.
This is just as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the *Aṣṭagrantha* is the Śīla-pāramitā; as the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the *Vinaya* is Mahāyāna study;

and as the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states that although the five divisions [of the Vinaya] differ, they do not obstruct the Buddha-dharmadhātu and Nirvāṇa. Thus, all of these take the precepts and discipline as their foundation.
The wondrous practice of the One Vehicle does not arise apart from wondrous understanding; how could it be otherwise? As the *Tiantai Zhiguan* says:
"Using the wisdom of the Middle Way, one universally enters into all phenomena. Thus, the Sūtra states: "Śikṣā, śikṣā" is the name for Mahāyāna precepts. Jingxi says:
"By means of this Middle Wisdom, one fuses all phenomena; therefore, every instance of stillness (*śamatha*) and activity (*vipaśyanā*) is none other than the Dharma-realm."

And so forth. One must understand that following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, all subsequent expositions and classifications of the teachings—whether shallow or profound—are without the slightest confusion.
As for their application to sentient capacities and their practice and veneration, the Great and Small Vehicles are harmonized and integrated, such that nothing is not perfectly sublime.

Therefore, one should know that our Patriarch’s propagation of the Vinaya takes wondrous contemplation as its core; it is likewise based on this principle. This is the very point upon which we should focus our minds, and it is something we must clearly understand.

I have frequently observed that while people lecture on the teachings, they are not adept at profound investigation; thus, the ancestral intentions have been neglected and lost. Therefore, I have briefly provided these citations, unaware that they might become overly prolix.

Next, regarding the specific intent: within the sections on the repentance of the six categories of offenses in the *Shishi yaolue chao* and the *Yi shu*, the ritual procedures for transformation and regulation are explained in detail.

In the *Śaṅgharāśi-lishi-chanfa* (The Ritual for Repentance Based on Both Principle and Phenomena), the regulations for the Vinaya (*jiezhi*) rely solely on the monastic codes (*vinaya*), whereas the methods of transformation (*huahua*) encompass both principle and phenomena, thus universally adhering to the sūtras and śāstras.

Furthermore, within the repentance of principle, it fully expounds the three contemplations (*sanguan*), thereby ensuring that both the prohibitions and transformations are observed together, and both principle and phenomena are put into operation.

Moreover, the "Śrāmaṇera" chapter of the *Shisao* (Commentary on the Essentials) and the "Receiving Precepts" chapter of the *Yeshu* (Sub-commentary on the Essentials) extensively detail the practices of both ordinary persons and sages.
The Dharma encompasses both the cultivation of merit and the cultivation of the Path. Furthermore, within the practice of the Noble Path, it fully elucidates three types of rational contemplation.

This is intended so that beginners may have a basis for their cultivation and practice, and find a place to settle their minds. Thus, the fundamental purpose of renouncing the world to study is not established in vain.

The fourth section, "Resolving Differences," is further divided into two parts: the general and the specific. First, regarding the general resolution concerning the three contemplations (*vipaśyanā*): Question:

Some say that the Nanshan school of teachings only transmits the characteristics of the Vinaya; why then does it present methods of contemplation? How should this statement be understood? Answer: This is not so. As Lingzhi said:
"The Tripitaka was established for the sake of a single person, yet it provides the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*). It is for the sake of a single person that one practices them."
Furthermore, it is said: "According to practice, although one may encompass both [self-cultivation and benefiting others], according to the teaching, each has its own specific domain.

How could there be such a thing as practicing the Way as a renunciant while specializing in only a single aspect, or compiling and circulating [the teachings] without clarifying both principle and phenomena?

Regarding the main body (*zhengzong*) of the various sutras, the modes of practice differ from one another; as in the *Xinshu* (New Commentary), which uses five criteria to refine and simplify them, ensuring there is no confusion or overlap.
