Receiving the Precepts Again, Father.
I presided over the ritual platform at Mount Jinfeng and have repeatedly performed and received the precepts.

Now, because the Japanese Master Jin has traveled afar by sea to investigate the Vinaya-piṭaka, it has become clear that while his conditions for receiving the precepts are well-established, there are slight obstacles; his regard for the precepts is not yet predominant, and he himself doubts the validity of his prior reception.
I earnestly beg for a further increase [in this work]. There are many in the world who are ignorant and who readily give rise to doubts and obstructions, thereby opposing his lofty aspirations.

Therefore, I have examined the Vinaya-śāstras and the explicit texts of the various patriarchs to resolve their delusions, so that the gates of the Teaching shall not be blocked. This is divided into three major sections. First, regarding the citations:

I first cite the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school, which does not establish the practice of receiving the precepts multiple times. The *Shisong lü shu yiji* (Commentary on the Ten-Recitation Vinaya), fascicle 1, states: "The Sarvāstivāda school..."
The precepts are not to be issued repeatedly, nor are they to be received repeatedly; offenses are not to be committed repeatedly. This is because one relies on the constant, original determination;

thus, the mind of an Arhat consists of precepts of middle and lower grades, and so forth. Next, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Cheng lun) is cited to establish the principle of receiving [the precepts] repeatedly.
The *Jiyao* (Commentary) cites the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, saying: "Some ask: 'Is there such a thing as issuing the Prātimokṣa repeatedly? The answer is: Within a single day..."
One receives the seven virtuous restraints (*śīla*). Wherever one attains the Path, one further acquires these restraints; those previously obtained are not lost.

They are designated by their superior forms. These seven virtues are: namely, the five precepts, the eight precepts, the ten precepts, the full precepts (*upāsaka-śīla*), the dhyāna-precepts, the concentration-precepts, and the path-precepts.

This is a shared precept (*sādhāraṇa-śīla*). Furthermore, the *Sarvāstivāda Masters and Disciples Biographies* states: "Receiving [the precepts] again increases them to the superior grade (*uttama*), yet the original reception is not lost.
The *Biographies of the Monks* records: "In the seventh year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the Kasmirian śramaṇa Guṇavarma arrived in Yangzhou."

He granted permission for the nuns to receive the precepts again, saying: "As for the categories of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*), they proceed from the subtle to the manifest.

If you wish to increase and clarify them, I greatly rejoice in this. In the tenth year of the Yuanxi era, Saṃghavarman (translated here as Zhòngkǎi, "Armor of the Multitude") conferred the precepts once more at the Jietan in Nanlin, the capital of Yangdu, for fifty monks including Huizhao and thirty-three nuns including Huiguo.
The Vinaya-holder, Dharma Master Huiyi, raised an objection, saying: "The sages and wise men of antiquity all shared a common standard; why do you alone alter it?
How can you withstand the expectations of the assembly? The Saṃgha replied: "The differences among the five schools have been the constant principle since this time.

We have collectively renounced secular life precisely for the sake of propagating the Dharma. Since the Dharma must necessarily be transmitted, how could it offend the sentiments of the multitude? He asked again: "Now, the precepts are not something that can be—"

This is a matter of appearance. Recently, I have observed those receiving the full precepts again; some follow their seniority based on their previous ordination age, while others take their current reception as the beginning.
This ambiguity between advancing and retreating is sufficient to cause deep doubt. I reply: there are two types of persons, and thus they are not of one kind.

If one’s years are not yet complete and the months of gestation are not yet fulfilled, then the current reception is taken as the beginning. If one’s years are already complete, then one enters [the order] accordingly.

Regarding the stage of the precepts: if one merely suspects that there were states of middling or inferior resolve when previously receiving them, one must logically seek to increase their excellence and receive the precepts again;
in this case, the original seniority (la) shall serve as the fixed standard. It is even said: "The precepts have nine grades; the lower serves as the cause for the higher."

As for those who seek [the precepts], their minds vary in quality, and the conditions upon which they rely also differ. There may be obstacles such as receiving them separately or generating the resolve anew.
The *Nanshan Dànyǐng* states: "On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Qiánfēng era, I..."
At the beginning of the summer retreat, once the *śīlakaṇḍa* (precept platform) had been established, they proceeded to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) according to the Dharma.

At that time, twenty-seven individuals who had previously prepared for it received the precepts together. The *Zhīyuán jí* states: "As for the precepts (*śīla*), they are the vessel and oars for crossing the sea of suffering."
It initiates the source of the myriad virtues; it is that which the sages and worthies of the Three Vehicles revere, and that which the patriarchs of successive generations have transmitted.

Yet, among those who receive it, there are differences in the clarity or obscurity of their minds and the refinement or coarseness of their studies, such that they cannot all be judged by a single standard.
Thus, there are those who receive it for the first time, and those who augment it further, and so forth.
Second, regarding the establishment of the doctrine, we must trace its origin to the precepts. These are, in essence, the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

While there are differences in the verbal teachings and their methods of instruction, when one grasps the intended meaning, the substance is in fact no different. One must know that every phrase is the very nature (*dharmatā*), and every phenomenon returns to the source.

It is as profound and remote as empty space; it is as deep and vast as the *dharmadhātu*. This is what is called the "profound precept of supreme goodness" and is also termed the "inconceivable virtue of the precepts. Yet, if one wishes to...

Regarding the recipient: one must simply know that they are equal to the measure of the Buddha. The Dharma reaches only the mind; mind and phenomena are perfectly interfused, and both objects and conditions are wondrous.

The perceiving subject and the perceived object are, from beginning to end, a single thought-moment. The three vows and the three clusters of precepts are identical in their preceding and succeeding aspects.

This constitutes the superior grade of mind, which alone accords with the superior grade of precepts. It accords with the original intention of the Tathāgata and harmonizes with the Perfect School of the Nanshan tradition. If, however, there is even a single moment of...
If there is even a hair’s breadth of obstruction, one cannot escape the reproach of those who value the Dharma; how could one avoid the charge of mere toil?

If the mantra is not encountered under the guidance of a worthy teacher or lacks the requisite conditions, one vainly bears the vessel of superior preceptual virtue and falsely receives the metaphor of the bright pearl.

Later, perhaps upon hearing the teachings one begins to realize it, or upon reading the scriptures one finally understands; remembering that one's prior reception was either inferior or non-existent, one sighs over the emptiness of past lifetimes.

To eliminate the void and lose what is lost, one must know what is not right and reform one’s errors; to perceive righteousness and act with courage, one must decisively increase one’s resolve for the Dharma. This necessarily relies upon the Ultimate Teaching. I reflect further:
the compassionate heart of the Great Awakened One benefits all beings; how could it be limited only to those present before him?

Since the net of the teachings covers the times, its reality extends even to the final age. Indeed, because there are differences in the transmission of Emptiness and Existence, the teachings of the Gate vary in what they exclude or retain. There are...

The school of the *Sarvāstivāda* (Sapoduo) was narrow and left this matter behind; how could it have required ascending [the altar] twice? The *Dharmaguptaka* (Sifen) attained a profound understanding of its universal application;

it did not insist solely upon receiving the precepts a second time. As the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "To attempt to regulate the laity while lacking a standard for governing the Dharma is the reproach of the *Sarvāstivāda*.

That human relations and the Dharma follow their proper order, and that the ritual applications are manifold, is the praise due to the *Dharmaguptaka*. Regarding the practice of receiving the precepts repeatedly in this land, the *Monastic Biographies* (Sengzhuan) provide extensive accounts.
I have clarified the *Commentary on the Platform Sūtra* by briefly extracting its essential points as previously presented, so that there may be a teaching upon which to rely.
However, a deeper understanding will only be realized by those of long-standing experience; this is what I feel in my heart.

Third, resolving doubts: A questioner asks, "Now you speak of 'receiving [the precepts] repeatedly. What is the precise meaning? According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the seven categories of precepts are each received separately; how then can one see the sense of repetition?
In the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* and the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, the ten and fifty precepts are also received sequentially; is this not also repetition? Answer:

The essential point of receiving [the precepts] repeatedly depends solely on the arising of the substance (*dravya*). The nature of this substance is profound and subtle, and there are differences in the tenets and systems of interpretation. It is as in the case of many...

In this treatise, it is argued that those with inferior resolve receive five [precepts], while those with superior resolve receive ten. Although the latter five are generated by a superior resolve, the former five remain inferior;

their substance does not increase through generation. Since their substance does not increase, one does not undergo a "repeated reception" (punar-upasampadā) regarding the former five. This is precisely the basis upon which that school does not establish such a position.
Even if all three sets of precepts were generated by a superior resolve, their three substances would necessarily differ in nature across time, because of that [inferiority].

That which is reckoned as the primary creator is matter (*rūpa*), and that which is created is also matter. Although it is not visible or resistant in the sense of being an object of sight, its essence is obstructive.

Thus, the *Ye shes snying po’i rnam bshad* (Commentary on the *Tattvārtha*) states: "However, because it is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they mutually obstruct one another; based on what can be differentiated, it is therefore called 'matter' (*rūpa*).

Because its essence is matter, it is not mutually pervasive; according to what it produces, each is individually restricted. Therefore, it is not said to be "repeated" (*punarukta*). It is established [as such].

In the school of True Emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*), karma is created by the mind; its essence and characteristics are empty and harmonious, transforming according to conditions. It receives its name based on the degree of intensity:

as for example, receiving five [offenses] with an inferior state of mind and eight with a middling state of mind—these, being intensified from the previous five, are all classified as middling grade. Receiving ten [offenses] with a superior state of mind is likewise categorized.

The preceding eight stages of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are likewise thus. Therefore, proceeding from a single essence, they arise in succession: increasing the small into the great, increasing the narrow into the broad, and increasing the inferior into the superior.
This is like adding waves to the ocean; the nature of moisture is no different, there is only a distinction between shallow and deep.
It is also like adding black dye to black; the substance and color of the garment remain the same, there is only a difference between the fresh and the old.

This is merely a distinction between them. That there is a "re-issuance" (zhòngfā) and a "re-reception" (zhòngshòu) can be roughly understood. Question: How are "re-issuance" and "re-reception" to be distinguished?

Answer: The *Zizhi* states: "Re-issuance refers to multiple precepts; re-reception pertains to a single precept. If this is so, why does the treatise clarify "re-issuance" yet mention "re-reception"? Answer:

It is because through the "re-issuance" of the substance (*ti*), one simultaneously obtains the "re-reception. This is due to the fact that those seven forms of reception constitute a single entity (*yītǐ*).

Because it was initiated [for that purpose]. Question: According to the teachings, there is a progressive increase, yet the ultimate tenet returns to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*. How, then, can you establish your doctrine by relying on the Perfect Vehicle (*paripūrṇa-yāna*)? Answer:

According to that school of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vāda*), even if one speaks of the "superior grade," it still belongs to a partial embrace [of the truth]. One must investigate the Buddha’s underlying intention and clarify the synthesis and convergence [of all teachings].

There is no dharma that is not wondrous; there is no precept that is not perfect. Regarding the aspiration for enlightenment as elucidated in the commentaries and sub-commentaries of our Patriarch, although three grades are listed according to the literal text and their underlying meaning, this is done for the purpose of comparative evaluation so that one may understand their relative depth and shallowness.
To thoroughly exhaust the Patriarch’s intent, one must rely entirely upon the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzhi*).
One wondrously gives rise to the superior mind (*uttamacitta*), vowing to evoke the perfect precepts; therefore, it is called "superior grade.

Within the *Chao* and *Shu*, when demonstrating the characteristics of the superior grade, it is consistently stated that one acts to fulfill the three clusters of pure precepts (*triskandhaka*) and, as taught, opens the breast to wondrously give rise to body and mind so as to universally encompass the subtle and wondrous wholesome dharmas of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The *Ji* states that this superior mind is contrasted with the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā-vipaśyanā*), further noting: "Such is the reception by the mind."
This refers to the immediate arousal of the perfect essence (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). What is now called "increased reception" must rely on the fundamental tenets of the Nanshan school:

only when one perfectly arouses the three minds and perfectly accomplishes the three aggregates does it constitute the ultimate, highest-grade (*adhimātra-adhimātra*) precept. Question: Within our ancestral teaching tradition, from the Tang dynasty until the present, it has flourished throughout the world.

Who would not know the profound meaning of the perfect arousal of the superior mind? How could there still be those who receive [the precepts] while remaining stuck at the middle or lower grades? Answer:

Although the teachings of the Dharma are manifest, the capacities of sentient beings differ. Some may be able to bestow instruction upon those who are meager and obscure, yet their methods of guidance lack regularity;

others, being ignorant and dull-witted, possess minds that are clouded and distracted. If even a hair's breadth of delusion falls away, there will be a deviation of a thousand miles. This is comparable to the Way of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius.

To instruct people in goodness—whether they be worthy or unworthy—is the constant way throughout both ancient and modern times; what is there to be surprised by? Question: Since the substance of karma is one, how can emptiness be anything different?

Answer: The Tathāgata teaches according to the capacities of beings; thus, regarding this single dharma, he may sometimes designate it as "form and mind," and at other times designate it as "neither of the two.

These various [designations] differ. The masters of the various schools have not grasped the Buddha’s intent; instead, they cling to the literal names as if they were the actual substance, each maintaining their own particular calculation.
This constitutes the fundamental tenet. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In my sūtras, I have sometimes spoken of it as form (*rūpa*), and the bhikṣus then said it was form;
I have sometimes spoken of it as non-form, and the bhikṣus then said it was non-form. All this arose because they did not understand my intention.

Thereupon, the Patriarch thoroughly investigated the Buddha’s intent and established the "perfectly penetrating substance," which is precisely the single seed of consciousness. Having thus grasped the Buddha’s meaning, [he realized that] mind and form...
It is not dual. To recognize the essence according to its names, one attains its reality in every case. When it is said that "this is mind," it refers to the substance of this karma;

for the entire mind is inherently complete, and all occurs solely through the mind. Since the subject and object of cognition, as well as the initiator and the initiated, are none other than mind, it is called "mind.
When it is said that "this is form," it is form that is identical to its nature, like waves that are identical to water. By realizing the true source of form, one reaches the ultimate limit of form.

To attain the true reality (*dharmatā*) of form is what was previously referred to as the "thesis" (*pakṣa*). Although one may obtain the name "form," because one does not know its reality, it is said to be "not two.
Since its essence is solely mind, it is called "not form"; yet because it possesses actual characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is called "not mind. As for the term "seed" (*bīja*):

However, these karmic seeds are inherently present by nature; they are manifested through the conjunction of various conditions, and because their essence possesses functional capacity that gives rise to manifold virtues, they are called "seeds.
This is the core point upon which Nanshan based his investigation of their substance. Question:

Since the circular body (the perfect reality) has already been received within the ritual arena, is it still necessary to further receive the Bodhisattva precepts? Answer: As has already been clarified in other texts, I request that you seek this out for yourself.
Question: The principle of receiving [ordination] again may be understood as before. However, since the substance of the karma differs, it must be reconciled for comprehension.

Furthermore, regarding one who receives [ordination] again, the circumstances are identical to those of a new entrant. How is one to decide their rank and seniority? Answer: As previously cited from the *Saṃgha*, this is very clear.
If the years of the previous ordination have already been reached, one follows one's original seniority; if the months and years were deficient, the current reception constitutes the beginning.

This is what one must study. Question: Since one has already received the precepts previously, committing a grave offense constitutes a "limit" (an anta); yet, if one originally lacked the precepts, it is difficult to avoid being considered a "thief-dweller" (corāvasika).

These two paths present an obstacle; how should one handle receiving the precepts again? Answer: As previously cited and shown, fortunately there is a precedent available that can be relied upon, followed, and applied.

The Buddha permitted receiving the precepts again precisely for the sake of the present age. That successive patriarchs have transmitted this practice is certainly not a groundless reliance. Seek [this method].

That statement is truly most agreeable. The Saṃgha maintains that [the lineage] must certainly be transmitted. Nanshan (Daoxuan) personally performed the consecration at the altar; Lingzhi (Zhiyi) composed the *Changshu* and presented it to Bing.
Yet, when the patriarchs practiced and received [the precepts], the era was already that of the Semblance Dharma; the capacities of beings were mixed, with the pure and the frivolous intermingled.

How could there have been none who violated the prohibitions against border offenses or those who resided as thieves? All the masters were manifestations of the four reliances, exhausting the source of transformation—how could this not be clear and difficult to dispute?

Regarding the presence or absence [of precepts] and whether one may or may not receive them: I have now compiled and excerpted from the *Platform Sūtra*, the *Monastic Biographies*, and the texts concerning the re-reception [of precepts], yet there is not a single sentence therein that mentions obstacles or hindrances.
Having carefully examined the intent of the various patriarchs, there must certainly be a reason for this; namely, as for the presence or absence of the precepts...

Whether such difficulties will be resolved or not, none can fathom; only a Buddha can know. Nevertheless, one must rely upon the teachings and, in accordance with the capacities of those before them, undergo [the precepts] again.
This is nothing other than a means of guiding and receiving others, all of which serves to establish karmic connections (*kalyāṇamitra*). Now, I shall cite various texts as evidence to clarify this:

the distinctions between capacities and natures, and the profound subtlety of the principles of karma, are such that as long as one’s wisdom has not reached the level of a Buddha, how could one dare to offer such arbitrary deliberations? When deluded persons encounter this, they are fond of [making such claims].
1. Ming. The *Qisheng zhuan* (Biographies of the Sangha of the Qi Dynasty) states that in the third year of Emperor Wen of the Wei dynasty, an *amogha-saṃgha* (unrestricted assembly) was convened.

The Emperor asked about the spiritual efficacy of the precepts received by the monks and nuns of this land, but none among the assembly dared to respond. There was one bhikṣu who requested to travel to the Western Regions to inquire of those who had attained the Way.
He then set out from Chang’an and traveled to India. Upon questioning an arhat, the latter replied, "I am but a minor sage; [I do not possess such knowledge]."

"Do you understand? Having said this, he immediately entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, and questioned Maitreya Buddha. The Buddha replied that he had obtained the precepts (*śīla*).

This clarifies that the attainment of the precepts is not something known by ordinary or inferior beings. As it says in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Resolving Doubts": "Good son, in the sūtras I have made this statement:
'If there is a bhikṣu who has committed the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), he is no longer called a bhikṣu. He is not... [the text continues].
Furthermore, it can produce the seeds and sprouts of goodness; it is like a scorched seed that cannot produce fruit.
When my disciples hear this teaching, they do not understand my intention and proclaim: "The Tathāgata has said that once the bhikṣus have committed a grave transgression..."
[Regarding] the loss of the bhikṣu precepts (this [view] is non-existent). Good son, in the sūtras I have spoken for Cunda of four kinds of bhikṣus:

first, those who have ultimately reached the Way (those beyond training); second, those who show the Way (those in the first three fruits of the path); third, those who receive the Way (encompassing both the internal and external).

The fourth is the defiled path (the stage of thinness). Generally, the four grave offenses constitute the defiled path. Having heard this teaching, my disciples were unable to grasp my intention and proclaimed:
"The Tathāgata has said that even if bhikṣus commit the four grave offenses, they do not lose their prohibitive precepts" (this is an adherence to existence).

Please examine the preceding text regarding the attainment and loss of precepts; those who possess [such views] are called thieves. How could one dare to judge [the Dharma] recklessly? Follow accordingly.

If one clings to these two views, how could it be possible to receive the teachings without being deeply wounded? Furthermore, the *Zhulin* states: When Dharma Master Zhìyán was still a layman, he had received the five precepts;

however, having committed some transgressions against them, he feared that upon leaving the household life and receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he would not have attained the precepts and thus his meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*) would not succeed.
He consequently traveled to Western India to consult those who had attained the Way. There, he also encountered an Arhat, yet he did not dare seek a definitive resolution from him. For...
Daoxian entered meditative concentration. When the Emperor inquired of Maitreya, he replied that Daoxian had obtained the precepts. Daoxian returned home filled with joy.

Observing this single episode, it is clear that although he had committed a transgression against the boundaries [of the Vinaya], it did not prevent him from obtaining the precepts. Thus we know that spiritual capacities vary between clarity and dullness, and aspirations vary between diligence and negligence;

whether one has committed an offense and its validity is established cannot be obstructed by a mere speck of superficial appearance, nor should it hinder the universal rule that has endured for a thousand ages. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "If..."

Committing the four grave offenses or the five heinous crimes, or slandering the Dharma, is called "breaking the precepts. However, due to certain causes and conditions, such a person may still be rescued.

If one dons the dharma robes, constantly maintains a sense of shame and remorse, gives rise to a mind that protects the Dharma, and establishes the True Dharma—of such a person I say it cannot be said that they have broken the precepts.
According to this text, a person who possesses shame and remorse is without fault even if they commit an offense, nor do they lose their precepts. Now...

Regarding those who receive [the precepts] again: they all give rise to shame and remorse, their faith and aspiration are profound, and even if they have committed transgressions, how could these constitute a terminal obstacle (*ānantarya*)?

If one insists that there must necessarily be the single difficulty of "living as a thief" (*caura-vāsa*), consider that the difficulty of living as a thief arises in the Vinaya because, due to hunger, one falsely assumes the appearance and robes of a monk, daring to participate in the recitation of the *Poṣadha* together with others, eavesdropping on the *Karmavācanā*, falsely claiming seniority by years of ordination, and rashly receiving [offerings].

To perform the ritual of giving [the precepts] while acting as a "thief-dweller" (a person who assumes the status of a monk through deception) is called being a thief-dweller. Those who have now left the household life harbor right faith in their hearts;

even if they hear the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), their intention is not one of theft. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, whether one is ignorant and dull-witted, or distracted by other thoughts such that one does not remember the beginning or the end of the ritual, none of these constitute an obstacle [to ordination].
Nowadays, those who have long remained within the gates of the Teaching are still unable to clearly understand the performance of the rites; how much more so for others who are merely superficial?

Some may become dull-witted; for what reason would their discernment be so penetrating? Some may be deprived by external conditions, such that there is ultimately no sequence between before and after. By citing and illustrating these cases, one may resolve doubts regarding the mind.
Furthermore, even when committing evil deeds or violating the precepts, the Vinaya still provides grounds for exemption; how much more so now, when one gives rise to a virtuous mind?

My courageous resolve increases ever further. In this present degenerate age, such [an endeavor] is truly rare. How could the Tathāgata’s teaching, which accords with the capacities of beings, lack a means to guide them toward the Way?
One must not stubbornly cling to difficult conditions and obstruct another’s high aspiration. Regarding the four reliances of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, they should be applied consistently.
I have here briefly set forth this explanation; may those who understand it discern its meaning. Written on a day in the winter of the Gui-si year of the Shao-ding era by Mi of Mount Ri.

The *Jiètǐ zhèngyì zhíyán* (Direct Exposition on the True Meaning of the Precept-essence) states: "The subtle matter is definitively existent; the partial penetration is definitively empty; the perfect penetration encompasses both emptiness and existence. This correctly reveals the Mahāyāna nature of the partial penetration.

The entire text and meaning of the first section, "The True Meaning of the Precept-essence," in the *Yèshū* (Commentary on Karma), from beginning to end, is entirely Mahāyāna and differs completely from previous [explanations].
The reiteration of emptiness and existence in the middle section is intended to cite ancient views and present their calculations, with the aim of refuting them decisively and manifesting the truth.

All the texts that effect this refutation originate from the Patriarch’s own mind and constitute the correct doctrine. However, because the meaning was still somewhat inclusive when he first addressed those calculations, he later established the Perfect Teaching to provide clear instruction;
it is only through the seeds of the *ālayavijñāna* that their actual nature is finally revealed.

First, according to the gate of conforming to existence (*sattva-dvāra*), its essence is discussed as being form (*rūpa*). However, among the various masters of this school (*nikāya*), first, some claim that its essence is constituted by body and speech;
second, others reckon that its essence possesses the capacity for benefit or harm, and thus they judge it to be form, as previously cited and demonstrated.

Although these [explanations] rely upon the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* and the *Abhidharmakośa*, they are none other than the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) taught in accordance with the capacities of beings. The various masters, failing to understand this, have instead established them as definitive tenets (*siddhānta*).
Consideration: Now, establishing the correct principle, we shall provisionally follow that calculation to resolve form by means of form.

This refers to the substance of karma produced by all sentient beings when performing good or evil deeds; its characteristics are manifest, and thus it is called "form" (*rūpa*). This is, in fact, the form of the mind-as-such which is identical to the nature (*dharmatā*);

it is subtle and difficult to know, beyond the comprehension of ordinary or limited beings. Only the Buddha-Tathāgata, whose various wisdoms are perfectly luminous, exhaustively penetrates this karma.

As for their nature, he knows it truly and sees it truly, and speaks according to reality. This reveals that although what was previously conceived is also called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*), one does not know its true essence;
therefore, he refutes it collectively, saying: "The mental discourse is thus."

In the provisional school (*prajñapti-naya*), both the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāvibhāṣā*) and the present Sūtra state that those of the highest grade must receive the Great [Vehicle]. Now, in establishing the essential nature (*svabhāva*) based on this reception, one must rely upon the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
First, the ancient calculations are briefly indicated; subsequently, the present position is demonstrated. Since karma arises from the mind, how could form (*rūpa*) be established by anything else?

Thus, all phenomena—internal and external, form and mind—are entirely the one mind, which undergoes transformation and construction according to conditions; hence it is said that "the mind divides to become form.
This reveals that the perceiving mind arises as its actual reality, while the instruments of body and speech are likewise empty and harmonious.

It is based on this great principle of the Vinaya that this teaching is presented. Since the creator is already harmonious and non-substantial, how could the substance of what is produced be anything other than so?

Second. For the time being, this follows the limitations of the teachings; thus it is said to be a "forced designation. Examining what follows below further clarifies the essence and function [of consciousness] and resolves the prior attachment to emptiness.
Although this relies upon the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, because that work merely represents a small teaching and a gate of emptiness, its intended meaning differs from that of the *Caturvarga-vinaya*.

That text states that "the mind creates," which is based on the six consciousnesses; now, however, we maintain that the essence of all phenomena is solely the one mind, which undergoes transformation and creation in accordance with conditions. As the text says:
"That which originally arises from the mind" means that its origination has a source. "Returning to permeate the fundamental mind" means that it finds its locus of support and maintenance.
Since the mind is both true and eternal, its essence is subtle and wondrous; therefore, it possesses the power and function of perfuming.

"The path of the mind is obscure and dark" means that the substance of precepts and karma is hidden and difficult to know (the substance is the karma of the mind, hence it is called the 'path of the mind'; as the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states that 'non-action' is designated as 'volition' to manifest the path).

[This refers to] what is called the "path of action" (*karmapatha*) and so forth. As for those who claim it can only be termed "pervasive" (*sāmānya*), these various masters [assert that] the essence of pervasiveness merely consists in following after names.
Therefore, by means of the term "and so forth," he restates the previous position to refute their ignorance. Although they say it is not dualistic, it is still an artificial construction.

Furthermore, within the preceding school, there was a direct determination of the substance of what is produced: formerly it was called "nominal matter" (*prajñaptirūpa*), now it is called "subtle matter. This is the nominalist school.

[In the] middle [section], it is resolved that the "ability to produce" (*nirmāṇa-śakti*) is manifested in what is produced. Formerly, it was held that the substance of the *kṛta-śīla* (the active precept) capable of producing [non-informative matter] consists of both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), whereas the *avijñapti* (non-informative matter) differs from this;
its substance was termed as being neither of these two. Now, it is resolved that the "ability to produce" resides in the six [bases].

Its arising must necessarily depend on eight [conditions]. As for the substance of that which is produced, how could it be a separate dharma? Thus, only then do we know the precise distinction between the producer and the produced. According to the various masters of the *Pratītyasamutpāda* school...

Regarding the five meanings of form and mind, when one exhaustively investigates the essence of karma, one finds no reality whatsoever. Therefore, it is further criticized by saying: "Not knowing what the designation refers to, one forcibly calls it 'non-dual'.
Jieyuan says: "This is provisionally attached to the meaning of expedient means; therefore, it is called 'forcibly designated. Furthermore, it says:

'Now, taking the meaning of the Way, when consciousness penetrates the appearance of the essence, one immediately knows that the two are non-existent. It is established by being provisionally attached to expedient means; therefore, it is merely called 'forced' (or 'artificial'). (As stated in that text). If [one realizes] the essence...

Regarding the provisional adoption of the general meaning: how could this apply only to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*? All Hinayana schools—whether in terms of doctrine or practice—are established based on provisional means (*upāya*).

If one adopts the general meaning, there is nothing that is not the single reality (*ekasatya*). Is it not the case that the "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*) of "form" (*rūpa*) in the various schools is merely a strong designation?

Now, I say this is not so. Both [instances] speak of "strong designation. The former is merely following the ancients; the latter is a refutation of error. Such is the intent of the text. Why must it be otherwise?

[The author] seeks [to clarify this]. It appears that prior to the Southern Mountain (Nanshan) school, the various masters who propagated the Vinaya did not comprehend the fundamental tenets (*mūla-artha*) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

They relied solely on the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*), which does not establish the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the two [precepts] through emergence. Therefore, he resolves this matter here. If this is so, what constitutes the essential nature of the correct doctrine of this school? Answer:

Since the "receiving" (*pratigrahaṇa*) already incorporates the "great" [precept], its nature emerges based upon that great [precept], as previously explained in the exposition. It is a mental seed (*citta-bīja*) produced by the mind and perfuming the mind; such is the meaning.

The reality is clearly manifest; however, because the teachings were limited in scope, it remained somewhat obscure within the texts. Later, the *Yuanjue jiao* (Perfect Enlightenment Teaching) was established to support and clarify the name "seed" (*bīja*). Question:

In the *Ji* (Commentary), the explanations regarding the mind giving rise to perfuming and so forth are all based on the six consciousnesses. How does this not contradict [the teaching of the *ālayavijñāna*]? Answer:

When explaining the meaning according to the text, one must not confuse the fundamental path of the school; the principle is indeed as such. This does not hinder the fact that the intent of the *Ji*'s author remains self-evident. As it says: "That is to say..."

This is precisely the point where the essence (*tattva*) is revealed; how could it be otherwise? One must understand that this section specifically investigates and brings forth the unconditioned (*avijñapti*).

Its essence is the seed of the mind, which definitively resolves the aforementioned ignorance. Please read the text carefully, and its meaning will become manifest of itself. Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya* states:
"The six consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, arise and perish without constancy; other consciousnesses arise in alternation, [and] perfuming (*vāsanā*)..."
The seeds cannot be established [as such]. The *ālayavijñāna* is neither born nor extinguished;

its essence is solely one, yet it is constantly perfumed by the six consciousnesses, such as desire, thereby forming worldly retributions and so forth. According to this text, it is determined that the six [consciousnesses] do not receive perfuming.
Since the present text speaks of "perfuming the mind" (*citta*), if one were to claim that the six [consciousnesses] are perfumed, I fear it would not accord with the intent of the commentary.

The Commentary (*Śū*) follows the provisional school (*jiazong*) in its ability to resolve the textual passage. It establishes a question-and-answer sequence as follows: "According to the *Zhengyi lun* (Treatise on Correct Meaning), that which perfumes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the seed;
it is capable of serving as a subsequent habituation (*vāsanā*). How can it be said that [the precept] ends when the body perishes and the precept ceases? Answer:

"The seed arises from volition (*cetanā*), and the formal undertaking is a vow (*praṇidhāna*). Since the vow is contingent upon the duration of one's life, the precept ceases when the body perishes. The practice arises in accordance with the vow, and its functional efficacy transcends [the physical form]."

Previously, it was stated that merit arises from volition (*cetanā*) and follows the mind without interruption; therefore, we focus specifically on its activity as that which can give rise to subsequent habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

This does not rely on empty vows to summon a pleasant fruit. The *Record* states: "The question regarding 'where they come from' is resolved by the later Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which determines that these two [types of merit] are not the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*).

Since consciousness would then persist eternally, the seeds would likewise never perish, which contradicts our school's principle that at the end of life, one loses [the basis for future existence]. Thus, [the former view] is incorrect.

It is difficult to interpret this as taking up a subsequent passage. (Regarding the text: If one were to say that it takes up the "Perfect" (yuan) teaching from later on, why not simply raise the objection there at the end of the Perfect Teaching?
Now, I maintain that this question follows upon the meaning of the preceding section on the Mahāyāna to raise an objection against the [opponent's] refutation.

Based on the preceding reliance upon the established tenets (*siddhānta*), when examining the essence [of karma] in terms of its magnitude, that which is capable of producing [results] and that which is perfumed (*vāsya*) is solely the single, true, and eternal [consciousness].
How could the essence of the karma produced [by it] perish along with the dissolution of the physical form? Such is the underlying intent behind this inquiry.

However, while the correct principle (*yukti*) establishes that the locus of reality lies precisely in the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna-bīja*), the previous adherence to the school’s tenets was expressed in somewhat obscure terms. Now, to provide a specific and definitive resolution, it says, "as in the Correct Principle," etc., thereby clarifying [the point].

This "perfuming of this life" is precisely the *ālayavijñāna*. This reveals that the essence of karma is the seed, thereby clarifying the meaning of its perpetual existence so that the intent of the question becomes distinct.
Furthermore, it enables the student to understand that what was previously termed "the capacity to resolve" (*nirṇaya*) is, in fact, the Great Meaning.

Question: Since the capacity to resolve is already the Great Meaning, why not speak explicitly of consciousness and seeds? Answer: Although the four divisions [of the *Vinaya*] are great, their teaching remains on the level of the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*). What is...
The phrasing is obscure, yet the meaning is clear. If this is so, then within this dialogue, you are explicitly discussing the seeds of consciousness;

is this not a confusion? Answer: If it were not explicitly stated, how could the intent of the question be clarified? Precisely because there was a fear of confusion, the question was established to provide a resolution. Question:
Since the seeds of consciousness are already discussed in this dialogue, why are they presented again in the subsequent Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao)? Answer: Within this dialogue...

Furthermore, to clarify the four divisions, within the final Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there is a comprehensive resolution of both emptiness and existence; thus, it is not precluded to present this again.

The remainder is as resolved previously. Question: In the commentary on the *Śāstra*, the explanatory text regarding the response concerning thought, vow, and practice all relies upon the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*. What is the meaning of this? Answer:
Regarding the explanation of the text based on its reception: although its meaning is sound, the underlying intent has not been clarified, which leaves many students in ignorance.

It must be understood that "contemplation" (*si*) refers to the mind capable of perceiving and receiving; "vow" (*yuan*) refers to the pledge to sever evil for as long as one lives upon receiving the precepts;

and "practice" (*xing*) refers to the resolve to uphold [the precepts] in accordance with that vow. If there is only contemplation and vow, but no mind of upholding, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-sarīra*) will not be generated.

As the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) explains regarding the "shared precepts" (*gongjie*) and "common precepts" (*tongjie*): "The former listing of 'shared' clarifies that the vows are received together; the latter listing of 'common' clarifies that the practice is followed together.

If, at the time of receiving the precepts, one discusses only the reception of the vows while lacking the intention to train in their practice, then it is merely a hollow vow and will not induce the attainment of the precepts.
Furthermore, the *Chao* (Sub-commentary) states: "If there is only the act of receiving [the precepts] but no mind of upholding them, then the reception of the precepts..."
"No. Furthermore, it says: "It is better to initiate practice than to seek through vows. Based on these various texts, one must maintain the mind for the precepts to be induced.
In the present text, because the period of aspiration has ended while the seeds of the precepts have not perished, it addresses the preceding objection.

Since nothing was actually obtained at the time of reception, how can one speak of their non-perishing? The first two lines of the text demonstrate the distinction between intention and aspiration; the subsequent two lines...

The "explanation" (*shi*) and "resolution" (*shi*) in the phrase "showing and explaining the period of vows" serve as a response; the "practice" (*xing*) below clarifies that the seeds of the precepts do not perish.

The single character "contemplation" (*si*) is identical to the "contemplative wisdom" (*sisi minghui*) mentioned in the *Commentary* (*Chao*), both referring to the person of perfect capacity (*yuanren*). It denotes the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as the faculty capable of perceiving and receiving [the precepts].

However, perfect understanding is subtle and profound; every movement of the mind and every stirring of thought is inconceivable. Since one receives the precepts with this very mind, what measure could there be to the essence of the precepts?
As for the merit of realizing this essence, its actual practice is paramount; hence it is said, "conduct follows [the essence]," and so forth.

Although the power of conduct is superior, when discussing its source, one must still rely on the subtlety of contemplation. Thus we know that sublime contemplation not only gives rise to the essence, but also initiates the merit of practice; both are [essential].
It is subtle and wondrous; therefore, it follows the mind of birth and death, continuing in an unbroken stream. Thus it is said, "The merit arises from equality," and so forth. Question:

The Sarvāstivāda school (Youzong) maintains that while the karma accumulated to induce rebirth resides in the *saṃskāra* (formative forces), its actual manifestation depends on the *anuvartaka* (concomitant factors). How does this differ in meaning from the present [text], which asserts that the capacity to initiate subsequent habitual tendencies resides specifically in the *saṃskāra*?

Answer: In the Sarvāstivāda system, the substance (*svabhāva*) lacks inherent power and function; the accumulation of karma is entirely dependent upon the concomitant factors. In this [present] context, however...
The essence possesses wondrous capacity, which is adorned by provisional practice; practice arises entirely from the essence, and the essence is accomplished through provisional practice.
If there were no merit in practice, the essence would be difficult to sustain to the end; therefore, it is said that [the text] "partially relies" on [practice], and so forth. Question:

Here it is said that "subsequent cultivation" refers to practice, while later it is said that "drawing out cultivation" refers to the essence. What is the meaning of this? Answer: This treatise discusses the survival of superior seeds of cultivation; therefore, it refers to [practice].

[The text] proceeds by first discussing the capacity for the cultivation of practice (*pratipatti*), and thus infers it from the essence (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, although this [cultivation] proceeds through practice, the entirety of practice arises from the essence;

and although one subsequently returns to the essence, the essence is established only through the mediation of practice. Please examine these two passages, and the meaning will become clear. Question:

Since the three mental states of intention (*cetanā*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), and practice (*pratipatti*) arise in succession without interruption, together perfecting the category of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), why does the commentary state that "the seeds remain" (*bīja-sthiti*)?

Regarding the mind of reflection (*cintā-citta*), the subsequent practice of inference is applied to the power of formative action (*saṃskāra*). It is not yet clear what the meaning is. Answer: This is most reasonable.

Furthermore, all wholesome and unwholesome formative actions are entirely created as karmic seeds by the single present thought-moment. When the mind is firm, karma is firm; when the mind is expansive, karma is expansive.
Now, because one perfectly receives the subtle and wondrous, its essence has no end. Since the essence is inexhaustible, its functional power is difficult to measure. Up to...

To manifest the essence and function [of the mind], one must rely on the adornment of the power of practice; therefore, one’s resolve to learn, cultivate, and uphold [the precepts] should be profound and firm.

From the very moment of first receiving them, one must not deviate for even a single thought-moment. Once received, one must guard against external objects as if facing an enemy, with no interval between moments of mind.
Through the power of inconceivable cultivation, which permeates and transforms successively, this continuity becomes inexhaustible. Thus, deluded karma is washed away, and the pure mind is revealed.
The essence itself becomes the fruit of sainthood; therefore, it is said that one does not rely on empty vows to summon a pleasant result.

Inferring from this, it can be seen that the power of practice transcends [mere aspiration]. Question: Both the Great and Small Vehicles speak of the "exhaustion of precepts" (*śīla-kṣaya*). What is the difference in their meaning?

Answer: According to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), both the practice and its substance are lost. Why is this? Because in that Lesser Vehicle, the basis from which [the mind] arises and that which is produced are both merely the six consciousnesses.
At the time of death, the six consciousnesses depart, their substance likewise perishes, and the continuity of practice is severed.

The Great Vehicle, however, maintains that the mind is complete and the mind creates. Although the creation occurs within the six, it arises fully through all eight [consciousnesses], like waves upon the ocean.
Since both the agent and the object of arousal are eternally abiding, what cessation could there be in their essence? It is only that the vows and practices cease when the physical form ends;

therefore, it is said that "the precepts cease. While the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ, the principle is as follows. The present question and answer are based precisely on the latter meaning. Question:

The ground is neutral (*avyākṛta*). The establishment of a boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) also gives rise to non-informative action (*avijñapti*). When receiving the precepts, one takes on the substance [of the discipline].

Why, then, must one discuss the mind of reception? Answer: The ground is neutral; its efficacy is attributed to the presiding agent. It requires the delimitation of boundaries through the power of collective mental activity to bring about the formation of non-informative action.
Receiving the precepts is not like this. Its substance is the foundation of the Path; it cannot be established by means of subject and object alone. Dharma is the root of practice; it is not...

Through what means are the transmission and reception [of the precepts] fulfilled? Therefore, in the *Sìshì chāo* (Commentary on the Four Categories) and the *Jiémó* (Karmavācanā), five conditions prior to receiving the full precepts are enumerated.
It is essential that the "capable" (the recipient) and the "object" (the conferrer) correspond; only then does the karma of non-informative (*avijñapti*) discipline arise. Does not the Sūtra say:

"The precepts are the vessel for crossing birth and death, the very root of the True Dharma"? One must have the convergence of conditions and their correspondence; if there is a violation, even if one has received them, they are not obtained. This is surely because one...
The cultivation of the Dharma-path requires that the preceding conditions be present; when the essence is complete and the practice perfected, the necessary conditions must be fulfilled.

One should know that the Dharma of the precepts has been transmitted from Buddha to Buddha and passed down from teacher to teacher. Such transmission is not in vain; it requires that the preceding conditions be met and that the recipient’s resolve be clear and distinct, for only then can the benefit of the transmission be manifested.
Receiving [the precepts] is not easily accomplished; one must clarify the mind and remain free from even the slightest delusion, for only then will the realization of the teaching be revealed.
"Receiving [the precepts] is not in vain. Is this not because the substance [of the precepts] is generated through receiving, depending solely upon the mind of the recipient?
Thus, the *Shishi yaoyong chao* states: 'As for the precepts, their merit lies in conforming to the vessel; as for the practitioner, their aim lies in internalizing and accepting them.

Only when one can thoroughly purify body and mind and receive [them] in accordance with the conditions does one attain the path of resonance. This text is clear; how could one remain ignorant of it? The *Shu* (Commentary) says:

Next, regarding the definition of the essence of the precepts according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): the precepts are the conditions for alerting the mind. Since beginningless time, ordinary beings have followed along with delusion to give rise to karma;
their movements have given rise to false associations, and they have lacked the thought to return to the source. Therefore, the Great Sage established the precepts to alert the mind.

One must not follow after delusions, lest one sink back into the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, it is said in the Vinaya: "To those who wish to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and exhaust the source of suffering, [the Buddha] would summon them and admit them into the ranks of the noble precepts.
Such individuals possess sharp faculties. Later, as the times gradually became turbid and corrupt, it was no longer possible to reveal this fundamental principle.
It then proceeds toward peripheral conditions and extensively opens up the pathways; ultimately arising from the mind, it falsely divides the external objects before it.

First, regarding "essence" (*tǐ*), this is the primary intent of this chapter (as indicated by the prior heading: "Second, setting forth the essence and characteristics"). However, this essence does not arise in isolation.

The attainment of the Dharma is necessarily achieved through its grasping. Whether the Dharma is partial or perfect, and whether its essence is coarse or subtle, arises from the differences in the attachments of sentient capacities.

Now, in manifesting the perfect essence, one must investigate the fundamental intent behind the establishment of the teachings and resolve the biased and limited attachments. When the subject perceives and the object arises within the mind, only then is that essence revealed;
it is, in fact, the seeds of consciousness. If one does not investigate the subtlety of the perceiver and the perceived, how can [the essence be realized]?
This concludes the brief summary of the circle of the means of accomplishment and that which is accomplished. To further explain this according to the text:

regarding "arousing the mind as the condition," this refers to inferring the efficacy of the precepts. "Arousing" (*cetanā*) is the meaning of the precepts; the precepts are that which arouses, and the mind is that which is aroused.

Although there are ten thousand variations in the arousal that guards against objects, the root of the formation of karma lies solely in the mind; therefore, it must be aroused. Although the text mentions the circle, the meaning [is as follows].

It penetrates both emptiness and existence. Regarding the "Existence School" (Yōsō), its admonition concerns the mind, yet it restricts only body and speech, for its prohibitions pertain solely to the seven branches [of physical and verbal action].

The "Emptiness School" (Kūsō) speaks of admonition, yet its prohibition lies in the heavy conditions [of the object]. This school [the Tiantai] encompasses the Great [Vehicle]; its prohibitions are identical to those of the ten karmic paths.

The discourse on admonition in the *Fahua lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) differs even more fundamentally from these. Since the capacity for admonition is already subtle, that which is admonished is likewise harmonious. Inferring the Buddha’s original intent, all that was established...

The teachings are none other than the Buddha-vehicle; how much more so when the sutras open and harmonize them, for diverse paths lead to the same destination. The wondrous precepts of the One Vehicle are ultimately perfect and luminous.

When a person of the Perfect Teaching upholds and observes them, both the capacity of the practitioner and the teaching are sublime. The ultimate and conventional truths operate in tandem, and both cultivation and nature are fully manifested.

How could these be considered merely superior deeds? They directly shatter ignorance. To have such an awakening of the mind—how can it be conceived by thought? Below, the meaning is categorized into three sections. First:

Seven phrases. First, "investigating the Buddha’s intention" clarifies the purport of the teaching. Next, "therefore, below," reveals the provisional bestowal of the Small Dharma according to capacities.

Third, "finally, below," determines that the Small [Dharma] is incomplete by reference to the perfect reality. Regarding the first of these, the phrase "returning to the source" means restoring the originally pure mind.

"Not following delusion" means that the intent lies in destroying afflictions. By means of the true meaning of the Mahāyāna, one deduces the merit of the precepts; this intermediate benefit is the benefit within the Small Vehicle.

However, they merely realize partial emptiness and do not understand the Middle Way. Because the seeds of their past-life karmic conditions for the precepts have matured, as soon as [the Buddha] once called out "Welcome," they received the Dharma in its entirety.
Since those of dull faculties are ignorant of "Mind-Only," the establishment [of the precepts] must rely upon external objects; thus, they receive them.

One must certainly rely on conditions and employ skillful means to establish the Dharma, thereby conforming indirectly to the capacities of those beings. Among the three types of sensation, one must resolve that the first two arise from within.

When one is deluded regarding the Dharma, the mind becomes divergent, and sensation enters from the outside; this is because one fails to realize that all sensations arise from the entirety of the mind itself. Question:

If it is said that sensation arises in dependence upon the mind, then would there not be no sensation at all even in the absence of various conditions? Answer: This is not the teaching of the Perfect [Vehicle]. You have surely not yet understood this.
Regarding the consciousness-mind and the principle of Mind-only: although it has not yet been clearly perceived, its meaning is set forth in the Patriarchal texts and is by no means obscure.
One should know that even the slightest thought of an ordinary person is vast, perfect, and harmonious, encompassing and pervading all things.

How could any conditions or the dharmas received from them exist outside of the mind? Since all dharmas are already the pervasive Mind-only, how could there be any conditioned phenomena that are not [Mind]?

It is mind-only. Thus, the reliance upon conditions and the reception of the Dharma both arise from the mind. Recently, some have claimed that within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), the ritual of receiving the precepts is not enumerated;
therefore, the practice of receiving them in the dharma-hall cannot be discussed as belonging to the Perfect Teaching.

This is because they do not understand the Perfect Teaching, which merely lies in the opening and resolving of capacities and teachings—wherein everything is nothing other than the single reality—thereby enabling the opening of wondrous understanding so that the reception of the precepts becomes ultimate. As for the conditions and dharmas, they are all...
Regarding the distinction based on the sutras: furthermore, since the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) is precisely intended to resolve the Small Vehicle, the *Ji* (Record/Commentary) instead states:

"This borrows biased texts to prove the Perfect Precepts. Since the biased is itself something belonging to the Perfect [Teaching], why must one speak of "borrowing"? How could it be called "citing as proof"?
My mind is not yet at ease. Question: Since this has already resolved the partial and small [teachings] for those of inferior capacity and the like, why resolve them again?

Answer: This was merely a resolution of the small dharma by means of the perfect meaning. However, those of inferior faculties do not grasp the intent of the provisional; they harbor divergent attachments regarding emptiness and existence that persist even after [the Buddha’s] passing.
Therefore, it is necessary to resolve them further. Question: In the previous third section, these divergent attachments were already set forth. Why are they presented again here?

Why is it clarified again later? The answer is: previously, I merely cited and indicated [the texts] to show that the past was not [ultimately] so; I had not yet manifested the definitive convergence.

Within this correct principle, the Perfect [Teaching] resolves the Small, and Wisdom resolves ignorance, so that both the capacity [of the recipient] and the teaching are exclusively perfect, ensuring that both the subject (the faculty) and the object (the teaching) are wondrous.

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "Foolish people consider [the two] to be different and, based on this, give rise to attachment, perhaps relying on form, mind, and so forth. The *Ji* (Record) states: "Foolish people" refers generally to all such reckonings;
alternatively, the latter two phrases specifically resolve the substance currently received. The preceding section clarified subtle matter (*sūkṣmarūpa*) and thereby refuted the Sarvāstivāda school;

now, this section resolves only the fourfold [classification] of manifest (*vijñapti*) and unmanifest (*avijñapti*) karma. (Question from the *Ji*): Regarding the substance of the precepts (*śīlaskandha*), what did the Master of the Record [Yuan Ce] maintain?

In this chapter, [the author] refutes Master Long’s false claim that the masters of the commentaries (*shu*) held that the three schools alternately rejected one another, for his meaning was quite clear. Now, the *Ji* states: "The *Dharmaguptaka* [vinaya] refutes the existence of subtle matter; the Perfect School (*Yuanzong*) determines that seeds have only a conventional substance (*jattie*). Is this not the alternating rejection of the three schools? Answer: Those who study the doctrines in antiquity did not examine the *Ji* minutely and misunderstood this passage, taking it to mean that [the three schools alternately reject one another]. It is not so. The meaning of the *Ji* is as follows: the *Dharmaguptaka* school refutes the Sarvāstivāda position on the existence of subtle matter; the Perfect School refutes the Sarvāstivāda position on the substantial reality of seeds; and the Three-Treatise School (*Sanlunzong*) refutes the Yogācāra position on the substantial reality of seeds. This is merely a case of the refutation of specific doctrines within the same school, not the alternating rejection of the three schools. Furthermore, the *Ji* subsequently states: "If one does not yet understand the intent of the Three Treatises, one will surely fall into the error of the existence of seeds. How could this be the alternating rejection of the three schools? Therefore, you should know that Master Long’s assertion is baseless. As for the statement in the *Ji*: "The *Dharmaguptaka* refutes the existence of subtle matter," this means that the *Dharmaguptaka* school refutes the Sarvāstivāda doctrine of the existence of subtle matter. "The Perfect School determines that seeds have only a conventional substance" means that the Perfect School refutes the Yogācāra doctrine of the substantial reality of seeds. "The Three-Treatise School refutes the existence of seeds" means that the Three-Treatise School refutes the Yogācāra doctrine of the substantial reality of seeds. Thus, these are all instances of refuting specific doctrines within the same school, not the alternating rejection of the three schools. You should understand this clearly. If you do not, you will fall into the same error as Master Long. Furthermore, the *Ji* states: "If one does not yet understand the intent of the Three Treatises, one will surely fall into the error of the existence of seeds. This indicates that the Three-Treatise School refutes the Yogācāra doctrine of the substantial reality of seeds. It does not mean that the Three-Treatise School refutes the Perfect School. Moreover, the *Ji* states: "The *Dharmaguptaka* refutes the existence of subtle matter; the Perfect School determines that seeds have only a conventional substance; the Three-Treatise School refutes the existence of seeds. This shows that the Three-Treatise School refutes the Yogācāra doctrine of the substantial reality of seeds. It does not mean that the Three-Treatise School refutes the Perfect School. The schools have alternately supplanted one another, continuing down to the present day; yet even you, my son, have not reflected upon this.

You do not realize that "subtle matter" (*sūkṣma-rūpa*) is a Mahāyāna tenet, and that the meaning of "subtle matter" and "seeds" (*bīja*) is identical. Subtle matter is definitively provisional matter, and seeds are definitively not dual.

Both cases are instances of using the Great [Vehicle] to resolve the Small; thus, they are not matters of alternating suppression. Such is the intent of the commentary—why do you not investigate this minutely? To leave it to mere arbitrary speculation is unacceptable.
Question: The *Ji* (Commentary) states that this passage resolves only the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya). What is the meaning of this? Answer:

The intention of the author of the *Ji* is that, regarding the Sarvāstivāda school’s [view of] provisional matter (*prajñaptirūpa*), it has already used subtle matter (*sūkṣmarūpa*) to resolve it; however, for the Mādhyamika school, which does not admit these two [types of matter], there has never been a formal resolution.

Therefore, he maintains that this passage resolves only the *Sifen lü*. Now, I shall further challenge this: since the establishment of the Perfect [Teaching] should pertain to the universal Perfect [Teaching] that encompasses both Emptiness and Existence, how can you conclude that it applies only to the *Sifen lü*?

Question: Does the essence [of the precepts] pertain exclusively to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*? Answer: It encompasses both the Perfect [teachings] and the schools of Emptiness and Existence; its principle is beyond words.

Since the present reception is based on the *Dharmaguptaka*, the essence of this superior-grade great reception is a seed of the mind. Because it is constrained by the limitations of the specific teaching, I have not yet dared to clarify it explicitly.

Therefore, when previously examining the essence, I merely stated that "the mind arises and perfumes the mind," which remains somewhat obscure in the text. Were it not for the definitive resolution of the Perfect teachings, how could one obtain the Dharma?

The substance is manifest and clear; having minutely examined the meaning of "round" (yuan), one then correctly resolves it upon the present reception [of the precepts]. (The *Ji* states: "It resolves only the *Sifen lü* [Dharmaguptaka Vinaya], which differs from my own intention.)

The Commentary further states: "When wisdom knows the conditions of objects, these are originally created by the mind. Not delusively conditioning objects—this 'knowledge through wisdom' refers to the perfect capacity.

It is clear wisdom that thoroughly penetrates; as for the conditions of objects, they are as indicated in the record. 'Objects' refers to the preceding objects, and 'conditions' refers to the dharmas of the precepts. 'Creating' means to fashion or construct.
One should know that whether it be objects or dharmas, they are fundamentally the one mind, which universally constructs according to conditions; therefore, both are called 'mind.'"

It is so. As the *Shuochao* says: "To contemplate that phenomena are mind—is this not indeed so? Furthermore, a sutra states: "All things are created solely by the mind. This is precisely that meaning.
Since all dharmas are both inherently possessed by and created by the mind alone, they are entirely mind. True Suchness (*tathatā*) is subtle and wondrous, perfectly interfused and all-pervading;
it transcends thought and discussion, being without marks and without form. The commentary seeks to sweep away deluded attachments.

Therefore, it is said that not falsely taking objects as conditions is precisely the True Truth (*satyārtha*); it is the submergence of all phenomena. Question: How is the meaning of "creation" (*nirmāṇa*) to be understood? Answer:

When one investigates that which is capable of creating, although it fundamentally consists of the six consciousnesses, it arises entirely from the eighth [consciousness]. Thus, it differs from the Lesser Vehicle teachings.

This act of creation is precisely the meaning of "following conditions" (*pratyaya-anuvartana*), which shall be seen in the following section. Sixth, as for "conditioned recollection," it is like an actor and also like a magical illusion.

The Master said: "The illusory appearances produced by the mind are mistakenly taken by the deluded to be real, while those who possess true knowledge say they do not exist. Question: The precepts and the teachings of the Dharma were spoken by the Buddha;

why then do you say they are created by the mind? Answer: All Buddhas preach the Dharma based constantly upon the two truths. All gates of teaching are established through provisional names within the ultimate truth.
Although the ultimate and the conventional differ, there is nothing that is not the One Mind. Since the teachings arise from this, [they are the work of the mind]."

It is said that the mind creates [all things]. Although precepts are established based on delusion, delusion is entirely identical to the True (zhen). Since the True and the conventional are mutually identical, how could they be separate from the One Mind?

Furthermore, it is said: "There is only the single consciousness which, following conditions, undergoes transformation; there is that [other] and there is this [self]. This clarifies that the True Consciousness follows conditions.

And it is pervasive; that which is called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) establishes all phenomena (*dharma*). Conditions (*pratyaya*) are precisely the mental thoughts of sentient beings, which constitute the conditions for the formation of karma.
True reality (*tattva*) is unimpeded, arising in accordance with thought. A record states:

"Not maintaining its own nature (*svabhāva*), it creates black and white karma according to defiled or pure conditions. This refers to not maintaining its own nature, meaning that its essence is unimpeded by principle; [it arises] through defiled or pure conditions.
This refers precisely to thoughts of good and evil. Good thoughts produce the human and celestial realms as well as the four noble stages; evil thoughts produce the four miserable destinies.
Thus, the ten realms—both the environment and its inhabitants—are created by a single thought. This is explained from the perspective of how causes elicit their corresponding fruits.

Furthermore, if one clings to thought as being truly existent, then the ten realms of environment and inhabitants will appear in chaotic profusion. However, if one realizes that thought is not [ultimately] thought, then subject and object...
Objects and conditions are equal and of one single mark. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "If one is free from deluded thoughts, then there is not a single object.
The *Sūtra on the Investigation of the Grounds for Awakening* says: "If there is no cognitive awareness, then there are no objects whatsoever.

Herein, I record the preceding meaning based on the perfect fusion of the three consciousnesses in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, to develop the practitioner so that they may contemplate delusion as being true and realize the waves as being [the ocean].

Water. Just as true suchness (tathatā) remains unchanging while following conditions, yet does not unite with delusion to become the true consciousness (amalavijñāna), so too does it remain unchanging while following conditions to manifest in conjunction as the manifesting consciousness (pravṛttivijñāna).
The remaining seven consciousnesses constitute the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (vastuvikalpavijñāna). Citing a scripture to provide proof, it says:
"For example, like the vast waves of the ocean, there are no diverse characteristics; so it is with all consciousnesses and the mind—difference cannot be found."

This means that by realizing the single thought-moment as perfectly interfused and subtle, the subject and object of cognition, the perceiver and the perceived, are ultimately of one mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
All phenomena have never increased, and this single thought-moment has never diminished. Thus, within this and that, one penetrates the absence of "this" and "that";
within differentiation, one thoroughly realizes the absence of differentiation. As it says below: "To realize delusion as such is itself the truth," and again: "Furthermore..."

When one knows karma and penetrates the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of karma through its formal practice, then cultivation is perfected within the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*). Thus, what is called "receiving" does not enter from without.
To understand in this way and to discourse on receiving in this way is precisely to accord with the Perfect Teaching and to bring the reception of the Dharma to ultimate completion.

Question: Previously you spoke of "objective conditions," and later you spoke of "following conditions. What is the difference in meaning between these two uses of the term "condition" (*pratyaya*)? Answer: The former refers to the precepts and the Dharma; the latter refers to...
"Mindfulness" (*citta-manasikāra*) refers to the meaning of "condition" (*pratyaya*). Question: By what meaning is the precept (*śīla*) designated as a condition?

Furthermore, what is the difference between this and the various general and specific conditions for receiving [the precepts] that precede it? Answer: The general and specific [conditions] serve as the conditions for receiving the essence [of the precepts].

The dharma of the precepts (*śīladharma*) serves as the condition for establishing practice and realizing the fruit. As the commentary states: "The precept is the condition for alerting the mind. Is this not so? Question:

The text above mentions "objects and conditions. Since "conditions" refers to the precepts (*śīla-dharma*), I do not yet understand whether these precepts and their objects are identical or different. Answer:

If one thoroughly understands that objects and conditions are ultimately a single reality and are nothing other than mere consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*), how could there be any distinction between self and other? However, when considering them in terms of specific phenomena (*vastu*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), identity and difference are not absent.
The object consists of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), whereas the precept is an institution established by the Buddha; it exists only as words and phrases, for its essence is not form.

The mind may be understood as distinct [from the object]. If Master Zhiguan says that "only names, phrases, and syllables remain, pervading worlds as numerous as grains of sand," (this refers to the *text*)—as in the case of the precept against sexual misconduct or the precept against killing, how could the precept itself be separate from its object? This is what constitutes their identity. Question:

Regarding the "receiving" (*śīlana*) discussed here, does it refer to receiving the object, or receiving the precept? Answer: "Receiving" refers to receiving the precepts; this is very clear in various texts. It is simply that the arising of the precepts...
It does not depart from its object. As the *Chao* (the *Shan-jian ji*) says: "The cause from which the precepts arise still pervades the dharma-realm.

Furthermore, as with the transgression of precepts—where a transgression must rely upon an object—here we discuss their reception; the precepts arise from the object. Thus, as this citation clarifies, the meaning is made even more evident.

It further states: "To comprehend delusive emotions, one must know delusive karma. These two phrases precisely describe the intent of receiving [the teaching]. "Emotion" (*qing*) refers to the sudden arising of delusive thoughts;
