Question: There are those who hold that the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) acts as the subject (*ālambaka*) and the mental factors (*caitasika*) act as the objects (*ālambana*).
What is the meaning of this? Answer: This is merely a skillful arrangement for the sake of poetic symmetry; it is not [the definitive position].

One must recognize that their meanings and purposes diverge, and that the distinction between subject (*grāhaka*) and object (*grāhya*) is fundamental; thus, each must be restricted to its own specific meaning.
Now, since the faculty of mind (*manas*) and the mental factors (*caitta*) are equal in their function of cognitive engagement (*ālambana*), how can one forcibly differentiate them? Question:

Some say that the faculty of mind (*manas*) as the sovereign mind (*citta-rāja*) is the subject, while the six consciousnesses and other mental factors are the objects. How is this to be understood? Answer: First, such a false differentiation of subject and object has already been refuted above.

Second, regarding the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras, as well as the literary compositions of the various masters, they all take the mind-faculty (*manas*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) as the sovereign, while taking volition (*cetanā*), desire (*chanda*), and attention (*manaskāra*) and so forth as the mental factors (*caitta*).

Their inclusion of the six consciousnesses among the mental factors is an extreme error. Question: There are those who take the seven minds as the subject (*viṣayin*) and the six sense objects (*ṣad-viṣaya*) as the object (*viṣaya*).
How is this? Answer: At first glance, this seems to accord with the treatises, for the treatises speak of "mind" (*citta*) and "mental factors" (*caitta*).

Regarding the statement that [the sense organs] operate upon their respective objects (*viṣaya*), even upon further examination, it is not tenable. Why? First, concerning the argument that the essence (*tattva*) and function (*vṛtti*) are simultaneous:

this is countered by the fact that the essence of the sense organ is distinct from the essence of the objective field (*ālambana*). Since this has already been excluded through analysis, why is there no careful scrutiny? Question:

The text excludes those that correspond to the essence and takes only those where the function is simultaneous. Why, then, do the five sense organs, the seven types of consciousness, and the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) span across both preceding and succeeding moments?

Question: Yes. Answer: First, the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) have matter as their substance; therefore, they belong to the category of obstructive phenomena (*sapratigha*). Furthermore, because they can produce consciousness to apprehend objects, they also enter into the sphere of objects (*viṣaya*).

Second, the seven types of mind and mental factors (*caitta*) enter into the sphere of objects by way of illuminating the boundaries of those objects; they also enter into the sphere of conditions by way of being able to cogitate upon them.

The five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are exclusively material and thus only enter into the category of the obstructive. As for derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), they do not [enter into the category of the obstructive].

It should be understood as follows: since its essence is not any of the three aforementioned [types of] objects, it does not fall into any of them. Question: Regarding the grasping of objects and the contemplation of conditions, how do their depths differ? Answer:

If discussed in terms of specific, delimited instances, the grasping of an object by the subsequent moment belongs to the category of "object-correspondence" (*viṣaya-pratighāta*). Continuous contemplation of conditions, however, constitutes "condition-correspondence" (*ālambana-pratighāta*).

If we discuss this in general terms: when grasping an object, how could there be no mental engagement (*ālambana*)? When there is mental engagement, how could there be no apprehension through illumination (*ābhāsana*)?

Thus, the two minds of apprehension through illumination and mental engagement arise alternately; however, the duration of apprehension through illumination is short, while the duration of mental engagement is long.

Apprehension through illumination is restricted, whereas mental engagement is pervasive. Being restricted, it pertains only to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); being pervasive, it engages with all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). Furthermore:

In the restricted sense, it refers only to present objects; in the comprehensive sense, it extends to the past and future. To distinguish them in this way is not without profound significance. Question:

It is said that all three types are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*). What is the meaning of this? Answer: Regarding "resistance" within the context of obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), "resistance" (*pratigha*) carries the sense of being hindered or obstructed.

The two pairs of "dhātu" (elements) and "āyatana" (bases) derive their names from their objects; however, because they function by taking up categories in common, the objects themselves are what must be distinguished.
Thus, it is known that the character *duì* (pair/correspondence) refers to a category (*lèi*), not to the sense of a "couple" or "pair. As detailed previously, is this not clear? Question:
Regarding the chapters and sections of various masters, what fault is there in definitively restricting the discussion to the subject (the grāhaka) and object (the grāhya)?

Answer: The faults are many; briefly stated, there are three types. First, obscuring the text; second, being ignorant of names and essences; third, losing the intent of the commentary (*śāstra*). As for obscuring the text:

the texts of the commentaries do not restrict themselves exclusively to the subject and object. Although they have counterparts, each serves to exclude [the other]. This is detailed as previously explained.

This shall be briefly indicated here. Regarding those who are confused about names and essences: "objective realm" (*viṣaya*) is established based on apprehension and illumination so as not to be confused;

"obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the confinement and blockage of material substance (*rūpa-dravya*); "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the calculation and deliberation involved in apprehension. When discussing names and essences according to their specific definitions, the essence reveals the name, and the name manifests the essence, without the slightest confusion.

If one were to discuss them by restricting oneself to the subject and object alone, then mind and matter would not be distinguished, and names and essences would become blurred and mixed. How, then, could they be manifested?

Regarding the substance of "provisional form" (*prajñaptirūpa*), those who have misunderstood the intent of the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā*) should consider this: the *Śāstra* presents three pairs of characteristics, which were not intended for any other purpose, but solely to reveal the substance of provisional form.
First, it is not a substantial entity that possesses obstruction; second, it lacks the capacity for illumination and apprehension; third, it cannot engage in cognitive reflection (*ālambana*).
It merely takes provisional form as its object, being subtle, hidden, and difficult to perceive; therefore, these three [characteristics] are used to represent and manifest it.
For example, in the Madhyamaka school, non-duality is realized naturally by investigating the non-dual essence of form and mind through five points in each case.
Yet those various masters failed to grasp this intent; they employed elaborate rhetoric where simplicity sufficed and took circuitous routes where directness was required.

Vainly wading through a profusion of words, one ultimately remains ignorant of the true nature of provisional forms. Having been deluded by oneself and leading others into delusion for how many years—who knows?
In the autumn of the Gengyin year of the Shaoding era, this emerged from Mount Rishan in Danchun.

The Receiving of Conditions for the Heavy Barrier (referring to relying on the precepts of goodness as the preliminary means; this constitutes one heavy barrier. Establishing the complete reception of the full ordination and practicing the subsequent reception of the Mahāyāna constitutes two heavy barriers.
This is specifically provided for clarification and resolution).

The *Shìchāo* (Volume One, Chapter Three: Receiving the Precepts) states: The *Vibhaṅga-vinaya* says: "I now resolve my mind to seek the Way" (when about to receive the precepts, one first sets forth what is intended).

"To seek the realization of the Way" (herein referred to as "seeking the Way") refers to the four fruits of the Hīnayāna. One should save all sentient beings; yet sentient beings all cherish their own lives (the Hīnayāna is exclusively devoted to self-benefit;

this is called "saving life," which appears to be altruistic, but protecting their lives is actually intended solely for one's own sake—to ensure that no harm is done to others is still self-benefit. Nevertheless, among all practices, protecting living beings is essential, and thus it is mentioned first).

Receiving [the precepts] on account of this matter constitutes the lower grade of a weak mind (one whose resolve is neither firm nor sharp, and whose heart lacks integrity). Furthermore, it is asked: "What is the middle grade? If one says:

I now direct my mind rightly toward the Way (to establish a resolve that is thorough and penetrating, utterly free from other thoughts; hence it is called "directing the mind. This is called "toward the Way. Compared to what precedes, it is superior; compared to what follows, it is inferior—as may be seen in the records).
Dispelling the doubts of sentient beings (The words regarding the dispelling of doubt do not represent ultimate deliverance; the characteristics of the middle grade can be seen herein).

I act as a bridge and ferry for all, being able to benefit myself and also benefit others (The bodhisattva’s benefiting of others has both deep and shallow levels; each of the various sūtras and śāstras has its own authoritative teaching).

Upholding the right precepts (What is expected by the aspiration of the mind is that the precepts follow the movement of the mind). It is also said: What is the superior grade? If one says, "I now resolve my mind and receive the precepts in order to accomplish the Three [Bodies]," [this is the superior grade].

Because it gathers the threefold aggregate of precepts (the superior grade of generating the mind, with the aspiration for the *jñapticaturtha* ceremony, one receives the three aggregates. Subsequently, prior to the formal *karmavācanā*, it is further stated: "Now I receive these precepts; I accomplish the threefold aggregate of precepts. This is called the superior grade of mind.)

Those who hold false attachments say: "The present *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act of fourfold motion) serves as the preliminary means for later [stages]. One should carefully examine this text. It leads toward the three gates of liberation and seeks the fruit of *nirvāṇa* (which consists of the two vows of abandoning evil and cultivating good).
Furthermore, by means of this Dharma, one guides sentient beings to reach *nirvāṇa* (which is the vow to deliver living beings).

This ensures that the Dharma remains long in the world (practicing the deliverance of beings and the protection of the Dharma; these three are the fundamental duties of one who has left the household life. Among these three, delivering beings is the most essential. Therefore, both this text and the *Karmavācanā-sūtra* cite the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating that one must give rise to a mind of compassion and focus exclusively on [this goal]."

To rescue and sustain sentient beings, before the third *karmavācanā*, he further exhorted them, saying: "Let your minds take as their object the rescue and sustenance of sentient beings, as well as the protection of the Buddha-dharma. Thus it is known that saving beings and protecting the Dharma are the personal responsibilities of the Saṃgha, so that the True Dharma may long abide in the world.

Now, one wishes to receive the precepts. If one does not first establish this mind, how could one be able to embrace the Dharma so as to encompass all things? How could one be able to give rise to practice so as to be universally extensive? Although the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure of a motion followed by three proclamations) is a minor ritual, because it gives rise to the Great [Vow], one immediately embraces the Threefold Aggregate (*trisaṃvara*). This is the meaning of our fundamental school’s doctrine that it penetrates the Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, the *Karmavācanā Sūtra* (Volume One, Chapter on Receiving Precepts, Prior to the Formal Bestowal of the Precept-substance) states:

The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* says that whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first be taught the Dharma to guide and awaken the mind, causing compassion to arise toward all objects of perception; thus, one obtains the *adhiśīla* (higher morality). [And so forth:

"Since you are free from obstacles and impediments, you will certainly receive the precepts. You should, in accordance with the treatise, give rise to the *adhyāśaya* (resolute intention), which is as follows:"

"Rescuing and gathering all sentient beings equally" (Examine this passage closely: it cites the *Śrāmaṇera-saṃvara-śikṣāpada-sūtra* to arouse compassion. This is specifically for the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of four announcements) for full ordination;

this constitutes the superior grade of mind by which one receives the superior grade of precepts. The method established in this sutra is identical to that in the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā*. The *Vibhāṣā* describes the arousal of the aspiration [for enlightenment] and lists three grades; the superior grade involves receiving [the precepts] once, directly embracing the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-skandha-śīla*). This sutra does not list the middle or inferior grades, but clarifies only the superior grade.

By citing the sutra to arouse compassion, it refers to the great mind of a bodhisattva, intending that one should immediately receive the great bodhisattva precepts. Within the text, there is no sense of arousing compassion as a preparatory means for a subsequent stage. Those in the world who speak erroneously on this matter have all failed to examine the text with sufficient care.)

The *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), Part 3, Lower (explaining the preceding scriptural text), states: "This dharma of the precepts is the fundamental task of those who have left the household life. It is not that those who have never harbored great aspirations are inherently incapable of containing it; there is indeed a profound reason for this.

This passage praises the scripture, citing the treatise to initiate the cultivation of compassion, which perfectly accords with the capacity of the practitioner and the teaching. The teaching refers to this very school, and its meaning corresponds to the Mahāyāna. In the *Chao* (Sub-commentary), it is stated that even one who belongs to the highest grade receives [the precepts] only once.

This clarifies the essential meaning: generally, in the practice of the Mahāyāna, the salvation of sentient beings takes precedence. Since sentient beings are provisional (*prajñapti*), one must understand the skillful means (*upāya*) so as not to stagnate in the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, but proceed directly toward Bodhi. Nevertheless, to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, one must first save sentient beings. Based on this principle of capacity and teaching, the ritual for receiving [the precepts] is established; therefore, one is first instructed to arouse compassion.

If one does not first arouse the great mind of compassion, how could one receive the Great Precepts of a Bodhisattva? This perfectly accords with the fundamental aspiration of leaving home; thus, it is said that there is a profound reason for this.

The text instructs one to arouse compassion toward the object because one practices compassion to rescue and gather in sentient beings (this explains that the arousal of compassion in the sutra and the reception of full ordination exist solely for the purpose of gathering in sentient beings). As it says:

The *Śīlasūtra* (Shanjie jing) and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-mūla* (Pusa jieben)—those versions intended for the seven classes of followers—are precisely these texts. (By citing these scriptures to demonstrate that when a bhikṣu receives full ordination, he simultaneously receives the bodhisattva mahā-śīla;

since it is permitted for all seven classes to receive the bodhisattva precepts, there is certainly no doubt that a bhikṣu receiving full ordination also receives the bodhisattva precepts. These three sentences constitute the words of the scriptural evidence.

People of the world do not understand this and falsely claim that the Patriarch [Daoxuan] ordered that one follow the sequence of the *Śīlasūtra* to receive them, asserting that the present method of receiving full ordination is merely a preliminary expedient. I have collated the commentaries on the sutra with the text of the *Vinaya-viniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā-śāstra* (Jiaoben shu), examining them minutely from beginning to end; such a meaning is nowhere to be found. Furthermore, as in the *Śāstra*, regarding the arousal of the three grades...)

The mind is entirely for the sake of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). How could a single superior-grade reception [of the precepts] conversely become a great preparatory means (*mahā-upāya*) for what follows? Furthermore, according to the Vinaya, the establishment of the ritual is for the purpose of accomplishing full ordination; yet, the arousal of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*) and the arising of compassion conversely constitute the "great" [preparatory stage] that follows. If it is claimed that this meaning is contained within the records (*vyākaraṇa*), [it is not so].

However, that which is established here relies solely on the texts of the Patriarchs to determine the Patriarchs' intended meaning; as for the records, they may be either correct or erroneous and cannot be indiscriminately adopted as they stand. If it were not for the preceding [state], how could the great [attainment] be admitted? The "subsequent" refers to this:

(this means that previously, in states such as "not yet harboring the Great," one regards the state of right reception (*samyag-avasthāna*) in relation to the arousal of the thought of enlightenment; hence it is called "preceding. When the arousal of the thought of enlightenment is regarded in relation to right reception, it is called "subsequent").

Question: Regarding the *Chao* (Commentary), what is the underlying scriptural intent for clarifying the three grades of generating the bodhicitta? Answer: It is based on the *Sifen lü* (Dharmaguptaka-vinaya). For this Vinaya’s principles encompass both the profound and the shallow;

since it establishes its teachings according to the fundamental doctrine, it distinguishes three grades. The lower grade consists of a single reception [of the precepts], which represents the meaning of the Vinaya’s inclusion of the shallow, and can be subsumed under the Gate of Existence (*yǒumén*).

The middle grade is precisely the fundamental Vinaya itself, representing the meaning of the Gate of Emptiness (*kōngmén*). Having already realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), [it proceeds to the higher grade].
They are harmoniously integrated without obstruction. However, the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) within this gate also encompasses both the profound and the shallow;

thus, the Master of the Commentary states: "Because they profoundly grasp the Mahāyāna meaning of emptiness, they are called Sautrāntikas and so forth. The shallow belongs to the middle grade, while the profound returns to the superior grade.

Furthermore, the meaning of partial correspondence (*pratisaṃyukta*) also encompasses both the profound and the shallow: the shallow includes the middle grade, while the profound corresponds to the superior grade. Thus, the middle grade is also...
This is the great meaning. Therefore, within the records (*jì*), it is contrasted with the stage of the small *bodhisattva* of "emptiness of mutual characteristics" (*xiāngkōng*);

the significance of this can be seen therein. The superior grade of the single reception is entirely Mahāyāna. Although it belongs to the category of "partial penetration," it ultimately penetrates the Buddha Vehicle (*buddhayāna*).

Thus, the *Chāo* asks: "What vehicle is the school (*zōng*) of this teaching that inspires the resolve for Mahāyāna? (This question precisely resolves the superior grade of the great reception. The answer is: "The school of these four divisions (*sìfēn*)."

The meaning corresponds to the Mahāyāna. The original text of the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "If there are those who, for their own sake, desire to seek the Buddha-way, or who dedicate [the precepts] to sentient beings so that together they may achieve the Buddha-way.
Based on this dialogue, it serves as: first, proof that the superior grade (*adhimātra*) is the primary doctrine with partial application (*pradeśa-prativedha*);
and second, proof that the superior grade is entirely Mahāyāna.
Question: Both the *Chao* (Commentary) and the sutra text cite passages from the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra* concerning compassion (*maitrī*). What is the intended meaning? Answer:

It is for the purpose of accomplishing the superior grade of receiving [the precepts]. The three superior vows constitute the three aggregates (*tri-saṃvara*); this is the resolve of a great bodhisattva.
Since compassion and salvation must necessarily come first, the treatise is cited to cause one to first give rise to compassion.
Question: The texts concerning compassion (*karuṇā*) and loving-kindness (*maitrī*) pervade all Mahāyāna scriptures; why then do you specifically cite the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*? Answer:

Since we are currently establishing the ritual for receiving [the precepts], we rely upon the Vinaya section; therefore, we cite the Vinaya treatises to demonstrate that within the Vinaya itself there is also the principle of compassionate salvation through the reception of the Great [Precepts].

Question: The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya-mūla-bhāṣya* (Duo lun) is a text of the Hīnayāna, yet it speaks of "compassion. What is the intended meaning? Answer: This is also a case of "partial universal application" (*fen-tong*). As the *Ji yuan* states:
"To apply the Small Vehicle for the sake of the Great Vehicle is nothing other than partial universal application. Therefore, within various schools, there are occasionally such intentions.

However, in the establishment of the teachings by the Dharmaguptaka school, the fundamental tenets are clearly identical. Here, the formal reception of the higher grade is fundamentally based on the principle of partial universal application. Cited.
That [text] attests to this; it does not conflict with our own position.
Question: The *Zizhi* states, "The superior grade of mind is intended to support the 'partially pervasive' (fentong) meaning of our own school. What is the intent of this? Answer:
Although this school’s partial transmission (*bentong*) is entirely Mahāyāna, it does not clarify the characteristics of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*) and receiving the Dharma;

therefore, it establishes the "superior grade" (*shangpin*) to clarify the generation of the three vows and the accomplishment of the threefold aggregate precepts (*trisamvara*), thereby manifesting the ultimate nature of the partial transmission’s reception of the Dharma.

Question: According to the Mahāyāna teachings, there are no more than two ways of receiving the Bodhisattva precepts: the sudden reception according to the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and the gradual reception according to the *Bhadrakalpika Sūtra*.

Now, if one receives the Great Precepts (Mahāyāna) based on the Vinaya, I fear this may result in a confused or improper practice. Answer: When the Patriarchs established these methods, they did so for two reasons:

first, to infer the underlying intent of the teachings; second, to embody the compassionate mind of the Buddha. How could this be considered a confused or improper practice? Furthermore, the distinctions between sudden and gradual, or Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, within the gates of the Dharma are all the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddha. The Patriarchs...

The Master said: "These are all teachings established according to the capacities of beings; one must seek their fundamental basis. Furthermore, the precepts transmitted by all Buddhas are solely of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna).

When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he likewise intended to take the One Vehicle alone as the foundation of his transformation of others. He received them instantaneously at the site of enlightenment."

The two vehicles do not receive it. Although the Deer Park bestowed the Small [Vehicle], their aspiration was solely fixed upon the Great. Because their wisdom was narrow and inferior, they were temporarily made to receive the Small;
had their wisdom been bright and sharp, they would not have hindered the reception of the Great. Even within the seating arrangements of the Small, there are those who obtain great benefit.
This is also due to the inconceivable power of the Buddha, which causes it to be so. Having attained such great benefit, one’s aspiration must necessarily become vast and far-reaching;

one does not become mired in the characteristics of dharmas, nor does one scheme for minor fruits. This is precisely the principle of the *Dharmaguptaka* school’s integration with the Mahāyāna. The Patriarch examined this intent of the teaching in detail.
How could it be restricted solely to the prātimokṣa? Therefore, one establishes the arousal of the mind of great compassion as the superior grade to receive the full precepts (*mahāśīla*).
Those wholesome precepts are intended for practitioners who enter the path gradually; furthermore, their intent differs from that of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

The latter is called "gradual" within the Mahāyāna, corresponding to the gradual approach of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*; whereas receiving the full precepts according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* is "sudden" within the Hīnayāna, corresponding to the gradual approach of the Hīnayāna itself.

The names are established according to their capacities; this is therefore what distinguishes them. As the *Ji yuan* (Explanations of the Source) states: "In the Provisional School (*jiàzōng*), one knows the provisional means (*quán*) yet does not abide in expedient methods (*fāngbiàn*).

This is precisely it. Question: Previously, it was stated that the *Yèshū* (Commentary on Karma) cites the *Śīla-sūtra* regarding the seven classes of practitioners receiving the Great [Precepts], using this as proof that a *bhikṣu* who has received full ordination is permitted to accept [the precepts]. Why is this?

Regarding the three clusters (*tri-skandha*): while those [precepts] received by the seven classes of followers in that sūtra belong to the stage of preliminary application (*upāya*), the present superior-grade reception directly incorporates the three clusters;
thus, their meaning differs from that [sūtra]. How can it be cited as scriptural proof? Answer: According to that sūtra, it says: "One who wishes to receive the bodhisattva precepts..."
First, one generates the mind of the Mahāyāna and receives the precepts of the seven assemblies.

Having already signaled the intention to receive them and having further resolved upon the aspiration of the Mahāyāna, although one may hold the fifty rules of the *Upāsaka-śīla*, it does not prevent one from spontaneously attaining the Bodhisattva precepts. That sūtra is intended for those whose faculties are suited to gradual entry.
Therefore, the seven assemblies are employed as a provisional means (*upāya*), while the subsequent upholding of the three clusters (*triskandha*) constitutes the ultimate goal.

The citation provided here does not refer to the meaning of those provisional means; rather, it takes the seven assemblies as the point at which one immediately attains the Mahāyāna precepts, thereby serving as proof for the present conferral.

Question: Once the three aggregates (triskandha) have been received under the recitation of the *jñapti-caturtha* motion, at what time are the various categories of offenses (*pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, etc.

acquired? Answer: Since the three aggregates have already been received, what dharma would not be included [within them]? (The characteristics of the three aggregates are as previously explained; they may be seen in the text of Master Meng’s response). How could there be a Prātimokṣa that is not fully possessed?

It should be understood that there are three categories of bodhisattva precepts: those received by renunciants constitute the renunciant precepts; those received by laypeople constitute the lay precepts;
the Brahmajāla Sūtra precepts apply to both laypeople and renunciants and are received by both assemblies; and the Śīlasamvara (Good Precepts) are received only by renunciants.

This is precisely the intent behind the citation of the *Śīla-sūtra* as evidence in the *Yèshù*. However, while it cites that text as proof, it does not rely upon it for the actual reception [of the precepts], as has already been settled previously.

Question: Since the superior grade [of precepts] already encompasses the three clusters (*tri-skandha*), why does the world say that one relies on the *kuśala-śīla* (wholesome precepts) as a preliminary expedient? Answer:
This is a false tradition from antiquity, resulting from a failure to examine the texts.

Now, I shall specifically cite the passages concerning the conditions for receiving [the precepts] from the *Chao* (Commentary) and the *Jingshu* (Scriptural Commentary), providing a detailed annotation so that students may understand that what the Patriarch established was not intended as a preliminary expedient for subsequent reception. Please investigate this thoroughly.
[The text] says: "Doubts will surely be resolved. Question:

Is the statement that "receiving conditions constitutes a great reception" the meaning of the Perfect (Yuan) teaching, or not? Answer: Although this superior grade belongs to the Mahāyāna, it does not yet constitute the meaning of the Perfect teaching;

rather, it is the "partial penetration" (fentong) Mahāyāna within our own school (*benzong*). Furthermore, the *Jiaochao* (Excerpts from the Scripture) is the preceding text to the *Yesu* (Commentary on the Essentials).

Although there are those who clarify the meaning of the Mahāyāna, these do not constitute a definitive establishment of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjue). Only the *Yili* establishes the Perfect [Teaching], wherein the Small Vehicle is integrated into the Great.
This is found exclusively in the section on "Establishing the Essence" (*chuti*) in the *Jieshu*. Yet, scholars of the lecture halls do not examine the text closely;
whenever they form words and sentences, they make no distinctions at all. This is truly lamentable.

Question: Regarding the condition of sensation (*vedanā-pratyaya*) being of the "superior grade" (*adhimātra*), if this does not accord with the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), why is it explained through the lens of the Perfect Teaching in the *Ji* (Commentary)?

Answer: The Patriarchs established these teachings with a specific sequence of meaning. Initially, they provisionally established the dharmas according to the [specific] school (*zong*); subsequently, they established the Perfect Teaching to provide definitive resolution and penetration.

If one examines the meaning according to the text, the preceding and succeeding sections are naturally distinct. However, if one uses the subsequent to resolve the preceding, then every dharma established in the former is none other than the meaning of the Perfect Teaching.

The Master of the Record (Jizhu), having already attained the perfect meaning (*yuan-yi*), does not hesitate to explain it through the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). This is so that those who come after may rely upon the practice of the Perfect [Teaching] to receive [the precepts]. Question:
Since the superior-grade Great Receiving (*shang-pin da-shou*) has already encompassed the Dharma exhaustively, what benefit is there in subsequently establishing the Perfect [Teaching]?

Answer: Although the superior grade is "great," it still belongs to the "partial penetration" (*fen-tong*). While its meaning may indeed be great, its teaching ultimately belongs to the Lesser Vehicle (*xiao*). Furthermore, the name of the superior grade is "Compassion" (*ci*).

The words concerning "compassion" both appear in the *Xiaolun* (Minor Treatise). Therefore, one must establish the perfect [teaching] to resolve the partial and the small; teaching and practice are then one, and the Buddha Vehicle is revealed.
This distinguishes the Great Ultimate as perfectly wondrous. Thus, the *Ji yuan* states: "In order to establish the meaning of the 'partially penetrating' (fentong) within our own school."
This is so. Question:

When the Patriarch established the Perfect [Teaching], did he do so to encompass both emptiness and existence, or was it solely the Perfect Fourfold [Teaching]? Answer: According to the treatises, when establishing the Perfect, it encompasses both emptiness and existence;
however, since the establishment of dharmas relies exclusively upon the Fourfold [Teaching], we therefore provisionally rely on what has been inherited as the "Perfect Fourfold."

Furthermore, the doctrinal meaning of the Four-Part Vinaya (*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*) encompasses both the profound and the shallow; thus, as soon as one has perfected the Four-Part Vinaya, one can simultaneously perfect the "Gate of Existence" (*yǒumén*).

Question: After establishing the "Perfect" (*yuán*) category in the *Yèshū* (Commentary on Karma), it cites textual evidence from the Vinaya that applies to all categories. In the *Jìyào* (Essentials), following the section on the "Superior Grade of Mind," it also...

Regarding the citation of passages that apply to multiple categories (*fen-tong*), it is not known what the underlying intention is. The answer is that the intentions behind the two cited passages are distinct.
In the *Chao* (the *Zichiji*), the text is cited directly (as previously quoted) to prove the "superior grade" (*shangpin*), which is precisely the meaning of applying to multiple categories.

In the *Shu* (the *Sifenlü Shanchi Shu*), it first reconciles them through the principle of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), stating that since both Mahayana and Hinayana are equally the mind, their ethical discipline (*lüyi*) does not differ; only then does it say, "How much more so for the *Sifenlü*, which clearly elucidates the Buddha Vehicle."

And so forth. This refers to using the Perfect [Teaching] to resolve the Small [Vehicle]; there is nothing in the Small that is not Perfect, let alone the Four Divisions [of the Vinaya], which clearly elucidate the Buddha Vehicle.

Since it uses the Perfect to resolve and reveal [the meaning], what room is there for doubt? Thus, the two citations in the *Chao* and the *Shu* differ as widely as heaven and earth in their intended meaning.

Question: According to our school’s tenets, even when establishing the precepts, there is no doubt regarding their subsequent reception; how much more so when the fundamental principles have been fully resolved? The core doctrine is extremely clear.

Yet nowadays, when approaching the moment of receiving the precepts, those on the high seat discourse at length, sometimes claiming that one receives them according to the sequence of the *Śīla-samuccaya*, or citing the analogy of the four-storied pavilion, or asserting that the Patriarchs established the "perfect" (enlightened) view while permitting the reception of the "small" (Hinayana) precepts as a skillful means to accommodate those training for the subsequent reception of the Great Vehicle.

Since your study has been shallow and your explanations fail to grasp the source, you have brought disgrace upon our school and caused no small harm. I request that you resolve these matters clearly so that the blocked mind may be opened.

In response: Having examined in detail the *Yuanzong Zhang* (Treatise on the Perfect School), I shall determine the rules for ordination, harmonize the objective realm with its conditions, and clarify the ritual procedures.
This reveals the practice that follows [the teaching]. There is nothing that does not clarify the meaning, harmonizing the teachings and practices, and sweeping away clinging attachments.

This enables one to rely upon the aforementioned ritual procedures, achieving perfect guidance and perfect opening, perfect reception and perfect upholding. When taking objects as conditions, it penetrates the three periods of time and spans the ten directions.
Do not depart from the present moment of mindfulness. To receive the Dharma is to immediately embrace the Three Vows and the Three Collections; it is simply this one "Mind-Only.

The five meanings are suddenly opened up, the partial and the pervasive are revealed, and the fourfold pavilion is finally seen. My Patriarch’s teaching gate is like the autumn moon suspended in the sky.
There is, then, no obstruction whatsoever. Question:

Some speak of the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna), while others speak of the "Three Aggregates" (Triskandha); what is the meaning of these? Answer: The One Vehicle refers to the vastness of the essence (tattva).

The Three Aggregates refer to the complete and exhaustive inclusion of all phenomena (dharma). Because it is ultimately expansive and universal, it is called "One. Because it provides the standard, sustains, and carries [beings], it is called a "Vehicle."
The Cloud Vehicle consists of the three aggregates of Dharma. Each and every one is ultimately vast and extensive; each and every one can serve as a standard for formation and provide transport.
Within differentiation, there is no differentiation to be found; within the possession of marks, the marks cannot be apprehended. It is subtle, wondrous, and perfectly interfused.
Beyond thought and beyond discourse: although this principle was present within the superior grade of the "receiving conditions" (*pratyaya*) discussed previously, it had not yet been fully revealed.

Only within the subsequent Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) is it definitively clarified that both receiving and following [the precepts] are nothing other than the mind alone; therein, the meaning of the three clusters (*triskandha*) as perfectly wondrous is finally manifested.
The phrasing has its sequence of priority, and the meaning has its degrees of depth;
one must investigate these minutely.
From the *Zhongnan Jiaye*, Volume Lower (Original).

Regarding the statement that "when both the mind and its application are maintained or violated, one incurs a transgression of the *prohibitory rules* (*zèzuì*), but when discussing only the transformative karma (*huànyè*), one does not incur a transgression of the *prohibitory rules*," scholars have all said this.
In the past, I also shared this view, providing commentaries based on transformative karma in works such as the *Huìyuán*. Now, upon examining these various texts, the meaning is as follows:

This is not possible. Since we speak of both upholding and violating the precepts, a violation necessarily entails the incurrence of guilt. However, regarding the practice of the teachings, one must apply them according to the specific situation;

one must strictly follow established ritual forms, rely upon the cultivation of remedial practices in the application of the mind, and maintain constant mindfulness. In these two aspects—upholding and violating—the characteristics of the teachings remain distinct and do not overlap.

Sins each have their respective destinations. Why not rely on the clear teachings instead of merely following one's own conjectures? Regarding the dual maintenance of both teaching and practice, this has already been clarified elsewhere.
Here, I shall briefly discuss the dual maintenance of the mind and its application. As stated in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), fascicle 1, upper:

"If we base ourselves on the application of the mind to clarify what constitutes observance and violation, then all precepts involve both types of observance and violation. What are these? Take, for example, the precept against sexual misconduct; it conforms to the prohibitive precepts."

"Prevention" (*fáng*) has the meaning of "restraint through observance" (*zhǐchí*). When the contemplation of revulsion manifests, one is free from thoughts of defilement; even if external conditions press upon one, one finds no pleasure in them throughout the three periods [of past, present, and future].
This is called "active observance" (*zuòchí*). To act contrary to what should be done is an offense of commission; to fail to act when one should refrain is an offense of omission.

(From the *Shùwén*) Following the prohibitions of the precepts reveals that one does not rely on worldly affairs to create objective conditions. Contemplating revulsion and being free from thought is precisely the application of antidotes and the gathering of mindfulness. The Record states: "In upholding any single precept..."
One must certainly give rise to a protective mind (*ārakṣā-citta*) with the aim of avoiding transgressions; this is called "accomplishing the observance of restraint" (*śīla-saṃvara*).

With the aim of initiating this protection, it is also "active observance" (*kriyā-śīla*). The same applies to both types of offenses. To commit evil in violation of the teachings means there is necessarily no counteractive measure (*pratipakṣa*).

(This commentary explains the characteristics of the mental application (*citta-prayoga*) in relation to the observance of precepts. In reality, this mental application is first universal to all precepts, and second, universal to all times.)
When upholding a single precept in relation to any object, it is entirely through the mental application of the two modes of restraint—abstinence and performance—that this is achieved.

If one’s conduct is not constant and disciplined, how could one remain untainted when facing objects? To uphold the precepts in relation to objects is precisely "restraint through abstinence" (*vāritasamvara*); this is a classification according to the teachings.

To give rise to the thought of guarding against the enemy is the "observance through maintenance" (shih-chih). To apply mindfulness so as to remain free from transgression is the "observance through cessation" (t'ing-chih). These two refer to the mental application (*citta-prayoga*).

In the *Shu-chi* (Commentary), it is stated that for every precept or phrase maintained, one maintains the precepts by being fully endowed with the conditions when facing an object; this refers to the "cessation-observance" (*nirodha-śīla*) according to the teaching.

It must be understood that both [types of observance] below involve the meaning of mental application. Readers must not confuse these terms like the characters "fish" and "ru. Regarding the phrase "to be free from faults," it means to be free from non-... [text ends].

To "cultivate mindfulness" means that the Vinaya prescribes the offense of a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for failing to do so; "arousing protection" refers to applying meditative contemplation as an antidote.
"Violating the teaching" refers to violating the various precepts as an antidote, as well as the rule of constant one-pointedness of mind, which serves to prevent transgressions.

"Committing evil" refers to actually committing an offense. Regarding the term "committing evil," there are both shallow and deep levels: the shallow refers to the arising of delusion through forgetfulness of mindfulness, while the deep...

According to this, committing an offense against an object is due to forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*). One should know that committing an offense against an object is likewise caused by not being restrained by forgetfulness.

Furthermore, the Commentary (Vol. 2, Upper) states: "Regarding 'antidotes' (*pratipakṣa*): in opposition to sexual misconduct, one trains in the practice of distancing oneself from defilement, such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*);
in opposition to theft, one trains in the practice of few desires and contentment; and in opposition to killing, one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) for all beings."

[The text says: "Practice. This refers to restraining oneself from falsehood and cultivating the practice of truthful speech, and so forth. (Commentary) This means to restrain one's conduct so as not to engage in what violates the prohibitions.

Furthermore, the Commentary (same location) states: "Arising of remedial practices" clarifies not violating the Dharma; this refers to the remedies for the various precepts, such as compassion and fewness of desires (which serve to avoid violating the Dharma).
Through the accomplishment of cultivation (the non-violating practice), one relies upon the non-violation of the Dharma to give rise to non-violating conduct. If, in this regard...

When the mind gives rise to aversion and indolence toward the Dharma, failing to practice constitutes a case where one relies on the "non-offense" rule to establish an offense (as stated in the *Śū-wén*).

Examining that *Śū-wén*, the first section concerns the rules regarding offenses, clarifying both offensive conduct and non-offensive conduct; the subsequent section concerns the opening [of the path] through non-offense rules.

This clarifies transgressions and non-transgressions. Subsequently, regarding the dharma of non-transgression through counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), it clarifies transgressions and non-transgressions.

As for the former two [categories], since they both rely on the established prohibitions of transgressions, how could they not involve counteractive measures? Why would they alone not discuss the prohibitions of transgressions?

This mention of "counteractive measures" is precisely what the previous commentary referred to as the meaning of "contemplation and revulsion. When the latter illuminates the former, then the functioning of the former mind is termed a "transgression," thereby clarifying the prohibitions of transgression.

Furthermore, the *Shu* (Commentary) [same source] states: "The [precept against] great falsehood allows for joking; the [precept against] sexual misconduct allows for pure giving; the [precept against] being separated from one's robes allows for the mental relinquishment (*smṛti-tyāga*), and so forth.
If one loses mindfulness in these matters, there is a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*). This is called 'offensive conduct. When one maintains self-restraint, it is called 'non-offensive conduct.

(From the Commentary Text) If one employs the mind in counteraction and the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, even if one suddenly encounters superior conditions, one will certainly not lose mindfulness. If one loses [mindfulness]...

"Mindfulness of minor transgressions" is surely not merely a mental application; it is a clear basis for regulation. The *Commentary* states: "One who loses mindfulness does not mean they are defiled by attachment to a prior matter;
rather, upon encountering such conditions, one must be all the more careful to guard oneself. To forget mindfulness is itself an offense.

(The text of the *Commentary*) Although the author of the *Commentary* uses these words, he has not yet clearly pointed out that the offense is a mental application subject to regulation. Consequently, from ancient times until now, there has been no settled doctrine on this point.
Furthermore, the *Sìshāo* quotes the Vinaya as saying: "The Buddha prescribed the maintenance of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Whether entering or exiting, bending or stretching, bowing or looking up, holding one's robes and bowl, whether eating or drinking, taking medicine, attending to the necessities of nature, or whether sleeping or waking, [the bhikṣu must maintain this]."
Whether coming or going, sitting or lying down, speaking or remaining silent, one should always maintain this single-mindedness. If one violates this regulation, one incurs an offense.

Furthermore, according to the *Mātṛkā-śāstra*, a bhikṣu of sharp faculties maintains mindfulness with every step as he enters his dwelling, with every morsel as he eats, and with every stitch as he puts on his robes.
One of dull faculties, however, performs the mindfulness collectively upon first obtaining food and clothing.
"Single-mindedness at all times" (from that text): to observe with constant single-mindedness at all times is another name for "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*).

Since it is stated that failing to maintain this constant state constitutes an offense, how could there not be guilt in violating the antidote? Furthermore, one must know that the antidote does not reside solely in the precepts;

constant mindfulness is not limited to robes and dwellings. Thus, the constant application of the antidote extends to all objects, both wholesome and unwholesome, and is enjoined to be practiced with single-mindedness.

The mind is that which gathers and protects. Although it is said that there are various objects, in function there is but a single mind. It is precisely within this single mind that observance (*dhāraṇa*) and transgression (*āpatti*) are manifested.

To maintain mindfulness through intentional gathering is "observance by action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*); to not violate the established regulations is "observance by cessation" (*virati-dhāraṇa*). (The "established regulations" refers to the texts in the Vinaya that enjoin the gathering of mindfulness.

To lose mindfulness and engage in deluded perception is "transgression by action" (*kriyā-āpatti*); thus to violate the Vinaya regulations is "transgression by cessation" (*virati-āpatti*). Transgression by cessation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for violating the teachings.

Committing a *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) is also [a case of] transgression. This refers to evil thoughts and subsequent volitions, such as looking at women with a defiled mind, as well as indolence, forgetfulness, and so forth;
all these constitute the commission of a *duṣkṛta*. To distance oneself from both types of transgressions is to accomplish the two forms of restraint (*saṃvara*);

the meaning is extremely clear. Question: What is the difference between this and the "dual restraint" of teaching and practice? Moreover, since the remedies are always present and all are governed by the Vinaya, how is it that we now rely on cultivation?

"Reverently" means to act in accordance with the teachings; is this not, then, the practice of the teachings? Answer: Although both rely upon the teachings, there are differences in how offenses are established. "Mental application" (*cittavṛtti*) refers to one's habitual state;

it reveals the dual aspects of upholding and violating based on whether the mind is diligent or lax, and based on whether one is in accord with or contrary to the teachings. "Practice of the teachings" (*śikṣācaryā*) refers to actions performed at the moment of an event;
it reveals the dual aspects of upholding and violating based on whether one is in accord with or contrary to the teachings. This precisely clarifies the meaning of mental application.

Regarding the mind: the practice of the teachings relies upon the Dharma. Just as there are three requirements for robes and alms bowls, and four conditions required for *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts), all matters concerning prohibitions and permissions within the Dharma have been established through formal composition.
One must strictly adhere to these ritual procedures (*dharmaparyāya*). Have you not seen it stated in the Commentary?
If one relies on the practice according to the teachings, it must depend upon an object to arise; to "rely on the teachings to practice" and act without transgression is precisely this.

The *Zizhi* states: "Holding both mind and action applies to all precepts; contemplating and cultivating the conditions for cessation applies generally to the karma of transformation (*huàjiè*), and is not part of the prohibitive teaching (*zhìjiào*).
That refers to the method of contemplative observation (*guānniàn*), which is the practice of the teaching of transformation. As the *Xingzong wen* asks: "Contemplative practice..."

[The opponent] says: "It belongs to the *vaipulya* (developed teaching). That is to say, it is 'prescribed' (*zhì*) by the teachings. Answer: The term "prescribed" (*zhì*) is indeed general; however, it can be distinguished based on the nature of the offense.

[In that text], the intention is that since the mental application merely incurs an offense against the developed teaching, the contemplative practice is therefore judged to belong to the developed teaching.

My current position differs. Although the teaching on mindfulness as an antidote belongs to the developed teaching, the Vinaya mandates that it must be practiced. To fail to practice it constitutes a violation of the prescribed rule, as previously cited and demonstrated. How could the meaning not be clear?

Question: The *Shu* (Commentary) states that "teaching and practice" (*jiaoxing*) means the sense of relying on the teaching to carry it out. Why, then, does the *Chao* (Excerpts) say that "teaching" refers to the Vinaya teachings and "practice" refers to remedial measures (*pratipakṣa*), which differs from the *Shu*?
I do not know what the intention behind this is. Answer: The authors wrote according to the circumstances; both versions accord with the Dharma. The *Chao* says:

"As for 'teaching,' it encompasses both teaching and practice. The *Ji* (Record) distinguishes between the two types of practice shared by the community: the practice regarding robes and bowls (*yibopxing*) and the practice of protection (*huhuxing*).

This is explained as follows: "Practice" (*caryā*) refers to the application of the mind for the purpose of counteracting [defilements]. "Recorded" (*vijñapta*) refers to clothing, food, and the four modes of deportment.

In the commentary (*śāstra*), it is fully elucidated that the application of the mind, the teaching, and the practice are integrated; thus, the subsumption of the teaching and the extraction of its meaning are two distinct aspects without any confusion between them.

The *Chao* (Commentary) does not distinguish between these two types; therefore, it subsumes them both under the two terms "teaching" (*jiao*) and "practice" (*xing*), each with its own specific intent.

Inferring from this text of the *Chao*, one point can corroborate what was stated above: that the mental application of teaching and practice are both defined by their phenomenal modes (*xingxiang*), such that they may either be contrary to or in accord with [the truth].
A second point can corroborate what was stated above: that "constant single-mindedness" (*chang’er yixin*) and "counteractive measures" (*duizhi*) share the same underlying meaning.

Furthermore, as in the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the teaching is categorized according to the three wheels; it specifically takes "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) as its basis for classifying the Vinaya Piṭaka.

This is because it adopts the meaning from within the Vinaya that the Buddha prescribed for bhikṣus to maintain constant mindfulness. This may also serve as proof for the preceding point regarding the "constant application" (*nitya-pratipakṣa*) of antidotes.

This applies universally to all; to violate it constitutes an offense. Question: The regulation regarding mindfulness and retention applies throughout both the sūtras and the śāstras, as in such passages as "reflect well" or "form this contemplation.
If this is so, then these teachings apply universally to both the monastic and the lay.
If a bhikṣu commits an offense, should the lay community also be considered to have committed an offense? Answer: Although the words of exhortation to remember apply throughout the sūtras...

Treatise: However, worldly affairs are chaotic and disorderly; transgressions therein are beyond one's power to control. Inferring from what the Buddha ordained, these were specifically intended for the internal community (the monastic order).
Moreover, the remedies [for such conduct] are constant: one must contemplate this, not that; one must keep this in mind, not that.

These matters are clearly recorded in the Vinaya texts as being strictly regulated for the internal community. Since these are formal regulations, violating them constitutes an offense. Worldly matters, however, are not subject to such formal regulation; therefore, violating them—[does not constitute an offense].

It is not in contradiction [with the precepts]. There is no fault whatsoever; thus, the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "The Way is contrary to the secular world; it constantly possesses temporal efficacy. It dispels worldly desires nearby and purifies all delusions from afar.

If one does not maintain it through mindfulness, how could one achieve thorough realization? (Text of the *Shu*) This clarifies that within the regulations, to violate them constitutes an offense; the meaning is thus made even clearer. Question:

Regarding the contemplation of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), is it a matter of phenomena (*dharma*) or of principle (*tattva*)? Answer: Generally, whatever the Buddha has established...

The teaching is intended to preserve the aspiration for renunciation. However, fearing that those of extremely dull faculties have not yet reached the principle of emptiness, they merely maintain mindfulness and collect their thoughts with a mind of conditioned activity, thereby accomplishing only formal ritual practice.
Even if they were to maintain mindfulness through the wisdom of emptiness, it would still not accord with the Buddha’s original intent.

It is essential that those of perfect faculties who have attained high realization—true and authentic renunciant bodhisattvas—illuminate [the truth] through the wondrous contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Every movement of thought and every stirring of the mind is none other than the ultimate, the realm of single reality; this is what it means to confine the mind within its proper sphere, and only then does one perceive the wondrous state of eternal suchness.
Question: Regarding the offense of losing mindfulness (*smṛti-pramoṣa*), how are the three schools distinguished? Answer:

This has already been briefly clarified in the commentary on the five examples and in the response to Master Reng. I do not begrudge you a glimpse of this. Recorded on the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa in the Gengzi year of the Jiaxi era.
Daily Record:
Distinguishing the Two Types of Cessation (*śamatha*), as well as the Meanings of the Eight and Nine Names, and the Single Category of Violations Regarding Cessation.
According to the texts of the *Śū* (Commentary) and *Chāo* (Sub-commentary), there are two designated names: first, cessation through non-learning; second, cessation regarding phenomena and matters.

The verses are divided into eight or nine sections, listing the offenses according to their root and branches. This clarifies the gravity of upholding or violating the precepts and provides a broad understanding of the clarity or obscurity of the mind.
Although the words and meanings are thus established, detailed study and discussion have been scarce; I shall now briefly explain them. The main outline is divided into two parts.

First, the two types of cessation-of-offenses (*nirodha-āpatti*) are clarified; next, the eight and nine phrases are distinguished. Within the first section, there are three parts: first, the citation of the source;

second, a brief explanation; third, the resolution of doubts. Regarding the first part, the *Chao* states: "Within the category of cessation-of-offenses, there are active offenses (*kriyā-āpatti*), such as when a person keeps extra robes beyond the permitted period."
Regarding the offense of building a dwelling without begging for materials, this refers to the offense of non-learning (*aśikṣita*) and the offense of non-action (*akriyā*).

The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "There are two types of offenses of cessation (*nirodha-āpatti*): the first clarifies the offense of cessation regarding matters and dharmas; the second distinguishes the offense of cessation regarding non-learning. It then provides a brief explanation.

The Master of the *Shu* relies precisely upon this text to divide the offenses of cessation into two. The structural divisions of the *Shu* are extremely clear. The first concerns matters and dharmas.

This refers to the legal procedures for both prohibitions and permissions. To clarify the role of the *śayanāsana-vārika* (the chamberlain), I shall cite specific precepts to demonstrate the principle that within cessation (*śamatha*) there is activity (*pravṛtti*).
Generally speaking, whenever one performs an action or cites a rule, upholding them constitutes "upholding both."

If one commits an offense, there are two types of offenses. Thus, violating the established rules of instruction constitutes an *āśraya-viruddha* (cessation) offense; engaging in improper practice constitutes a *kriyā-viruddha* (action) offense.

These two offenses arise from a single matter. Cessation is a single grade of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); action varies according to the gravity of the specific category (*varga*). Action is subsumed under the preceding position, while cessation is included here.

Both exist because of matters and dharmas, and are therefore termed "matters and dharmas" (*vastu-dharma*). (This cessation offense refers to the simultaneous maintenance of both teaching and practice.)
This constitutes a transgression that interrupts [the practice]. Regarding the "unlearned": first, upon descending from the ritual platform, one violates one's original vow;

either the mind suddenly abandons the good, or arrogance gradually arises in seeking [worldly things]; or one’s contemplation of the teachings and practices remains unclear, or one is muddled when engaging in cultivation during critical moments.

Being unlearned and ignorant, both offenses are incurred. It is precisely because of a lack of learning that these transgressions are committed, thereby summoning these two offenses. This is called being "unlearned."

This concerns the offenses committed by those who have studied versus those who have not. However, among those who have not studied, there are differences in the clarity of their wisdom and the gradual or sudden nature of their mental development.

Regarding all matters and dharmas, there are three levels of mental states—certain knowledge, doubt, and ignorance—which differ in degree. Therefore, these two types of offenses are examined across the four modes of conduct and the two sets of nine [categories] to reveal the characteristics of their lightness, heaviness, presence, or absence.
This is intended to make known that the net of transgressions is difficult to escape, and to ensure that one understands how to identify and repent of offenses without error. (3)

Resolving Doubts. Furthermore, there are two parts. First, resolving the matter of the *dharmas* (practices). Question: Regarding the statement that "non-practice constitutes an offense of omission (*zhi-fan*)," this is seen in the cited text of the *Commentary* (*Chao*).

As for the "offense of omission regarding the *dharmas* of practice," from what text does it originate? Answer: The *Commentary* states: "To fail to cultivate the practices in accordance with the specific matters [confronted] is termed an offense of omission. Furthermore, the *Sub-commentary* (*Shu*) states:
"When one is confronted by specific matters and *dharmas*, yet remains indolent and fails to cultivate them, all such cases are termed offenses of omission," and so forth. Thus, this is based on...

The titles [of the precepts] are established; there is not even a hair’s breadth of falsehood. Question: Regarding the practice of cultivation through questioning and responding, what is meant by "ceasing" or "transgressing"?

Answer: This demonstrates the dual meaning of maintaining and transgressing both the teachings and the practices. A brief explanation was seen previously; a detailed account is found in various texts. Question: If one is indolent and does not cultivate, that is simply "ceasing."

"Non-cultivation does not involve 'doing. How can this cessation (śamatha) be said to include 'doing'? Answer: The term "non-cultivation" applies both to "doing" and "not doing. This refers specifically to active construction;
therefore, to violate the established rules of the teachings is precisely what constitutes non-cultivation. Is it not just like [the prohibitions against] begging or speaking? The *Xingzong* says:

"Regarding the phenomena of formal acts, one commits an offense through cessation; thus, regarding wholesome formal acts, one violates the principle of 'not doing. (Text) This is also the same meaning. Not...

It may be subsumed [under the category of "committed offense"]. Question: May the categories of "matter" (*vastu*) and "dharma" (*dharma*) be termed "committed offenses"? Answer: The essence of a committed offense (*kṛta-āpatti*) extends to both wholesome and unwholesome matters and dharmas.

Although it extends to both wholesome and unwholesome, from the perspective of the meaning of "committing," they are one; therefore, there are no different designations. They are simply designated as the single category of "committed offense" (*kṛta-āpatti*) and "ceased offense" (*vārita-āpatti*).

The treatise distinguishes the meaning of offenses into two categories: first, ignorance regarding the practice of the teachings; second, intentional violation of the disciplinary regulations. Based on this distinction, two headings are established.

I pray that you will investigate the intent of the Patriarchs; it shall certainly not be in vain. Next, we resolve the case of "not learning. Question: Does "not learning" result only in an offense of omission?

Question: Does the principle of "non-learning" apply to unwholesome matters as well? Answer: If one commits the fundamental offense of sexual misconduct or theft, one further incurs the two offenses of "non-learning" and "ignorance.
How could it not apply? Question: Does the principle of "non-learning" apply to both types of observances (the prohibitive and the prescriptive) when one merely fails to train?

Answer: As stated previously, "non-learning" and "ignorance" apply across all four modes of conduct and the two sets of nine [precepts]. How could it not apply? However, there are distinctions in the degree of observance, which must be explained in detail according to their meaning.

One should know that only by skillfully upholding the sharp tools [of the precepts] does one truly earn the title of "learner" (*śaikṣa*). Should doubts or misconceptions arise, these are all permitted so as not to constitute an offense;

however, ignorance resulting from a failure to study results solely in the transgression of the rule against not studying. Furthermore, there are three grades of such individuals who do not study, as fully elucidated in the commentaries (*śū* and *chāo*).

There is no need for further elaboration here. Although one may not have studied, if they cease improper conduct when confronted with an object, they do not commit the fundamental offense; this is also called "upholding the Vinaya.
This does not preclude being ignorant regarding the teachings and practices, nor does it mean that one has attained a state of "unlearned ignorance" (*aśaikṣa-ajñāna*).

Should you not yet have attained understanding, I shall provide a further detailed exposition. As for the phrase "eight phrases corresponding to the teaching," this refers to contemplating the characteristics of the teaching in advance regarding the matter at hand.

The ancients held that because the Sage did not establish training rules (*śikṣāpada*) for unwholesome matters, the categories of "abstaining from what is maintained" (*virati-dhāraṇa*) and "committing what is transgressed" (*āpatti-karaṇa*) were generally permissible [to be left unregulated]. It is acceptable. Regarding wholesome dharmas, the Noble Ones have established that they must be studied; there is nothing that cannot be studied. Now, it is said that both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas are to be studied.

To become confused or forgetful when confronted with these matters cannot be achieved without study. Therefore, whether something is or is not to be studied encompasses all four modes of conduct, and this principle extends throughout the entire Dharma-realm.

As for the analysis of the four difficulties (*catur-durghaṭa*), I have already distinguished them; do not hesitate to examine this. This principle can be seen in the "Section on Penetration and Obstruction" (*Sengji tiaoshi*) of the *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao*, which discusses penetration through the dual aspects of teaching and practice, as well as the application of the mind. One must understand this regarding upholding and violating.

Chapter One: The Intent of the Various Sections. Regarding the meaning of the dual aspects of observance and transgression (*dhāraṇa-vilopa*), one should consult the "Section on the Nature and Characteristics of Observance and Transgression" in the *Śūchào* (Commentary) and the "Section on the Penetration and Obstruction" in the *Chão* (Excerpts), where these matters are fully and clearly explained.

As for the various rules of phrasing, if one examines them in relation to the fundamental precepts and traces them through the three mental states (*citta*), contrasting them with the cases of non-learning and ignorance to reveal the characteristics of their presence or absence and their lightness or gravity, then by dividing them in this manner, one will gain a rough understanding of the path. Question:

If one falsely practices a single matter, how many offenses does one incur? Answer: There is the offense of false practice, the offense of violating prohibitions, and furthermore, one incurs the four offenses of non-learning and ignorance;
thus, all are complete. Moreover, the four categories of offenses have their own gradations: two for the *dhāraṇī* (retention) and eighteen for the *vinaya* (discipline).

Furthermore, the eight clauses regarding the cessation of offenses only manifest the branches and do not list the roots. In two cases of offense, both the nine roots and the branches are listed together.

Regarding the clauses on the gravity of the offense according to the secondary factors (*anuvyañjana*), the Dharma does not depend on this meaning. As for the branches, they are established according to the different divisions of the three mental states (*citta*).
Consequently, if there is certain knowledge (*niścaya*), there is invariably no offense; if there is doubt (*vicikitsā*), both cases constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing). Not...

Regarding the consciousness of the mind: not learning the rules for forming offenses constitutes a *pāyattika* (offense of ignorance). Furthermore, there are cases where an offense is permitted or where it is formed; these are all seen in various texts.

One can say that the characteristics of maintaining and violating the precepts are indeed profound. Unless one has accumulated study to penetrate the subtle, exhausting the obscure and exhausting the principles, this meaning is difficult to perceive.
Written while serving as a guest at Lingzhi Monastery during the second month of winter in the third year of the Baqing era.
The *Shu shi shi chao chi fan pian tong sai wen chao* (Commentary on the Text of the "Chapter on the Penetration of Obstacles" in the *Chiji fa shi chao*) states:

"If one approaches practice to understand 'abiding in restraint' (*zhizhi*), it means to exert oneself in maintaining restraint when facing external objects; this constitutes practice. Herein, 'abiding in restraint' is specifically based upon encountering various adverse conditions."

This refers to those who rely on the observance of precepts (*śīla*). It differs in meaning from the "moon" [analogy] used for the two types of *śamatha* (cessation) and *dhāraṇa* (maintenance) within the practice of the teaching for those of inferior capacity.

For example, regarding the cessation of killing and stealing, because one first cultivates practices such as compassion and few desires, and thereby brings the practice to completion, it is called "observance through action" (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*). In comparison with... [the former].
When the object does not give rise [to transgression], it is called "maintaining through cessation" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*). This means that within cessation itself there is action.
Ceasing killing and stealing is compliance with the prohibitive precepts; cultivating loving-kindness and so forth is the arousal of contemplative antidotes (*vipaśyanā-pratipakṣa*).

If one wishes not to violate the precepts when encountering objects, one must have cultivated the power of these antidotes during ordinary times. Because the power of the antidotes has been perfected, one does not act toward evil.

Therefore, it is said that one does not give rise [to thoughts] when facing objects. This means that through the practice of *samatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight), one does not depart from *samatha*.

Thus, it is said that within *samatha* there is *vipaśyanā*. "Calm abiding" (*samatha*) refers to remaining free from transgressions when confronting objects; "insight" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the application of the mind for counteractive measures.

Furthermore, one must know that there are two types of *samādhi* (concentration): first, practicing in accordance with wholesome matters; second, not violating prohibitions—this is *samatha*, which leads to the following *vipaśyanā*.
The treatise states that it is "universal" (*sāmānya*). Second, regarding adverse objects, one accords with the precepts and abandons faults; this is precisely the position [of this stage].
Its function as a mental application for upholding is universal, as can be seen above.
If one explains "active maintenance" (*kṛta-dhāraṇā*) in terms of practice:

this active maintenance refers to wholesome activities and wholesome dharmas that are permitted by the prohibitions; it is called active maintenance because one practices with diligence in accordance with the teachings.

While its name is the same as the "active maintenance" in the preceding section on *śamatha*, the meaning differs. The former concerns the arising of insight (*vipaśyanā*) through the function of the mind, whereas the present one is based on responding to specific objects.
Dharma consists of acting in accordance with the teachings.

For example, when one wishes to recite the *Prātimokṣa* or perform a *karmavācanā*, first ceasing external conditions and aiming to remain free from gross transgressions is called "stopping" (*śamatha*).
Subsequently, performing the practice well is called "acting" (*vīrya*). Thus, within the act itself, there is stopping.
Reciting the precepts and so forth are the teachings received through formal instruction. Stopping external [distractions] and so forth are the cultivation of remedies.

Although the phenomena of practice are numerous, I shall cite for now the recitation of the precepts and the *karmavācanā* (ritual procedures), as these are constant practices. When people engage in social interactions, they may become indolent or commit evil; these are collectively termed "external conditions.
By regularly recollecting one’s original vows and vowing that all good must be practiced, one's conduct becomes firm; therefore, when facing [such circumstances], [one remains steadfast].
Regarding various matters, one is able to cease external conditions. Looking at the specific dharmas corresponding to each situation, there is a subtle cessation that is free from faults;
this is what is called "coarse" in contrast to the general cessation of ordinary times. Herein, acting according to the teachings means practicing in reliance upon the teachings.
Cessation belongs to the function of the mind, whereby external conditions are stilled. Through the power of cessation, action is accomplished. Action...
It does not depart from *śamatha* (calm abiding). Therefore, it is said that within the practice of *vīrya* (exertion) there is *śamatha*.

If one discusses the penetration and obstruction in detail, this mental application of maintaining through *śamatha* can naturally be compared with the previous mental application of maintaining through *samādhi* (concentration) to discuss their mutual penetration. This thus encompasses both cessation and maintenance; furthermore, it applies equally to both cessation and performance.

The author of the *Chao* (Commentary) provisionally treats them as mutually complementary, and therefore discusses the commonality between the mental application of cessation-maintenance and the ritual practice of performance-maintenance.

Regarding "committing an offense through the mind," there is also the cessation of such offenses. This refers to cases such as when a person commits evil without having previously trained in the good; these are of this class.

The preceding sentence [of the treatise] applies generally, while the following explains the specific meaning. Committing evil is "active transgression" (*kṛta-āpatti*); conversely, practicing according to the above is "cessation and maintenance" (*śamatha-dhāraṇa*).

Regarding acts such as killing and stealing, it is when the necessary conditions are fulfilled that an offense is established. "Non-learning" and so forth refer to offenses of omission (*virati-āpatti*).

Reversing the aforementioned [category of] omission constitutes commission (*kriyā-dhāraṇa*), which refers to the lack of cultivation of counteractive practices such as compassion and fewness of desires.

An offense of commission is based on the violation of the precept itself, whereas an offense of omission is based on the mental application; since commission is established through omission, commission thus encompasses both [commission and omission]. Question: This...
